section: Theory: Constructing Cross-Trait Summary-Statistic Matrices (SSY and Nmat)
text:
Theory: Constructing Cross-Trait Summary-Statistic Matrices (SSY and Nmat)

Overview
In multivariate Bayesian linear regression using summary statistics, the likelihood depends on cross-trait quantities of the form
\[
\mathrm{SSY}_{t_1,t_2}
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t_1,t_2}}
y_{i t_1} \, y_{i t_2},
\]
where (y_{i t}) denotes the phenotype of individual (i) for trait (t), and (N_{t_1,t_2}) is the number of individuals jointly observed for traits (t_1) and (t_2).
In the univariate case this reduces to the usual sum of squares (_t = i y{it}^2), but in the multivariate case the full matrix
\[
\mathrm{SSY} = \bigl[\mathrm{SSY}_{t_1,t_2}\bigr]_{t_1,t_2=1}^{n_t}
\]
is required to estimate or sample from a residual covariance matrix (E) or its inverse.
When individual-level data are unavailable, we must reconstruct or approximate SSY and the effective sample-overlap matrix (N) from summary statistics, phenotypic variances, and (estimated or assumed) phenotypic correlations. This section describes the statistical foundations of these reconstructed matrices and how the helper functions build_SSY_full_overlap(), build_Nmat_full(), and build_Nmat_frac() implement them.

Phenotypic Variance From Summary Statistics
For trait (t), let

(yy_t = i y{it}^2) (the univariate summary statistic),
(n_t) be the number of individuals with observations for trait (t).

The empirical phenotypic variance is approximated by
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(y_t)
\approx
\frac{yy_t}{n_t}.
\]
This is valid when phenotypes have been centered (or approximately centered), a standard preprocessing step in GWAS pipelines.
We collect these into a diagonal variance vector:
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2_y = \left( \frac{yy_t}{n_t} \right)_{t=1}^{n_t}.
\]

Phenotypic Covariance From Correlation Information
If we know (or estimate) the phenotypic correlation matrix
\[
R_y = \bigl[r_{t_1,t_2}\bigr],
\]
then the corresponding phenotypic covariance matrix is
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(y)
=
\bigl[ r_{t_1,t_2}
      \,\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(y_{t_1})
              \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(y_{t_2})}
\bigr].
\]
This step is essential: correlation matrices contain standardized information, and we rescale them back to covariance units using the variance estimates derived from summary statistics.

The Sample-Overlap Matrix (N)
For two traits (t_1) and (t_2), define
\[
N_{t_1,t_2}
=
\text{number of individuals observed for both traits}.
\]

Full-overlap assumption
When the two traits originate from the same biobank or cohort, the overlap is often close to the size of the smaller sample:
\[
N^{\text{full}}_{t_1,t_2} = \min(n_{t_1}, n_{t_2}).
\]
This defines the function build_Nmat_full().


Fractional-overlap assumption
In meta-analysis or multi-cohort settings, sample overlap may be partial. We then model
\[
N^{\text{frac}}_{t_1,t_2}
=
p_{t_1,t_2} \,\min(n_{t_1}, n_{t_2}),
\]
where (p_{t_1,t_2} ) is a user-supplied overlap proportion. This defines build_Nmat_frac().
The diagonal entries satisfy (N_{t,t} = n_t).

Reconstructing the Cross-Trait SSY Matrix
The cross-product between two traits is defined as
\[
\mathrm{SSY}_{t_1,t_2}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t_1,t_2}}
y_{i t_1} \, y_{i t_2}.
\]
Under the assumption of independence across individuals and using the covariance identity
\[
\mathbb{E}[y_{t_1} y_{t_2}]
=
\mathrm{Cov}(y_{t_1},y_{t_2}),
\]
we obtain the summary-statistic approximation
\[
\mathrm{SSY}_{t_1,t_2}
\;\approx\;
N_{t_1,t_2}
\cdot
\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(y_{t_1}, y_{t_2}).
\]
This is the key identity used by build_SSY_full_overlap():

it constructs the covariance matrix using (R_y) and the variance estimates,
multiplies by the appropriate overlap counts (N_{t_1,t_2}),
and forces the diagonals to match the observed univariate summary statistics: (_{t,t} = yy_t).

Thus, the reconstructed SSY matrix is:
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{SSY}}
=
N \odot \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(y),
\]
where () denotes elementwise multiplication.

section: Why SSY and Nmat Are Needed in Multivariate BLR
text:
Why SSY and Nmat Are Needed in Multivariate BLR
In a multivariate Bayesian linear regression model
\[
y = Xb + e,
\quad
e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, E \otimes I),
\]
the full residual covariance sampler for (E) requires access to the cross-trait quantities
\[
\sum_i e_{i t_1} e_{i t_2},
\]
which, after substituting (e = y - Xb), depend on the observed SSY matrix, the cross-products involving (X), and the current posterior draw of (b).
When individual-level data are unavailable, the only way to compute these cross-trait sums is through a reconstruction of SSY and Nmat from summary statistics.
Without these matrices, the sampler must be restricted to diagonal residual variances (the usual summary-statistic assumption).
The functions provided here therefore enable full multivariate residual variance estimation in summary-statistic MTBLR when a phenotypic correlation matrix or sample-overlap information is available.

Summary

build_Nmat_full() constructs a full-overlap sample-overlap matrix
(N_{t_1,t_2} = (n_{t_1},n_{t_2})).
build_Nmat_frac() generalizes this using overlap fractions
(N_{t_1,t_2} = p_{t_1,t_2}(n_{t_1},n_{t_2})).
build_SSY_full_overlap() combines variances, phenotypic correlations, and overlap counts to reconstruct:
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{SSY}} = N \odot \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(y).
\]
These matrices provide the necessary inputs for a full sampler of the residual covariance matrix (E) when only summary statistics are available.

5.1 Deriving SSY from first principles
Let (Y_t) be an (n_t)-dimensional vector of observations for trait (t).
If samples overlap partially, define the set of shared individuals:
\[
\mathcal{I}_{ts} = \text{indices of individuals with both }y_t\text{ and }y_s.
\]
Then:
\[
\mathrm{SSY}_{ts}
=
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_{ts}} y_{ti} y_{si}.
\]
If we assume:

random missingness independent of trait values, and

covariance structure homogeneous across individuals, i.e.
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(y_t, y_s) = \sigma_{ts}
\]

then the expectation becomes:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SSY}_{ts}]
  = |\mathcal{I}_{ts}| \, \sigma_{ts}.
\]
If we approximate the overlap size as:
\[
|\mathcal{I}_{ts}| \approx N_{ts},
\]
then:
\[
\mathrm{SSY}_{ts}
\approx N_{ts} \, \sigma_{ts}.
\]
Estimating (_{ts}) by:
\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{ts}
= R_{y,ts}
  \sqrt{
    \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(y_t)\,
    \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(y_s)
  }
\]
yields the final approximation:
\[
\mathrm{SSY}
\approx
N \odot \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(y).
\]
This provides a principled summary‑statistic reconstruction of
(Y^Y) suitable for multi‑trait Bayesian models.

section: Workflow Scripts as Executable Architecture Documents
text:
Workflow Scripts as Executable Architecture Documents
A workflow script serves several roles at once:

It demonstrates a complete object handoff across public functions.
It records marker-order, sample-row, scaling, and LD settings that must remain consistent.
It provides an integration check that independently developed package layers compose correctly.
It supplies compact inspection patterns for objects that may contain tens of thousands of marker rows.

It does not replace function help, automated tests, or a study-specific analysis plan. Help pages define individual arguments. Tests should verify small deterministic contracts. Workflow scripts instead show how realistic, potentially expensive pieces are assembled.
Before running either workflow, replace its local data paths, confirm the selected sample and marker order, choose an LD output prefix that can be written safely, and decide whether the demonstration-scale MCMC settings are appropriate for the immediate purpose.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
BED-Direct and Summary-Statistics CSR Workflow
sparse_ld_bed_workflow.R is the practical bridge between an individual-level BED model and a summary-statistics CSR model. The complete data and alignment contracts are documented in Sparse-LD and BED workflows.
Its stages are:
BED-backed Glist + phenotypes
    -> align LD markers with BED columns using cls
    -> optionally fit stblr_bed_marker()
    -> compute stats with bed_xtx_xty()
    -> stream sparse LD with sparseLD_stream_CSR()
    -> fit stblr_csr()
    -> compare BED and CSR summaries cautiously

Prepare BED, Glist, and Phenotype Inputs
The workflow loads a qgg Glist, selects chromosomes and markers, and obtains or simulates a phenotype matrix. mtsim() is useful for integration checks because its returned effects and causal markers provide known truth. In a real analysis, phenotypes and covariate adjustment must instead follow the study’s analysis plan.
The script maps selected LD-marker identifiers back to BED marker columns:
cls <- match(Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]], Glist$rsids[[chr]])
stopifnot(!anyNA(cls))
This is a correctness check, not bookkeeping. The same selected markers and order must be used for BED fitting, sufficient statistics, sparse LD, and posterior interpretation.


Optionally Fit the Direct BED Model
stblr_bed_marker() reads marker data from BED files during fitting. It is the direct individual-level comparison path and does not need a separately prepared sparse-LD artifact.
Use it when individual-level genotypes remain available and direct marker updates are desired. Record the selected rows, cls, scaling choice, prior settings, scheduling controls, seed, and MCMC settings. These choices matter when comparing its output with a CSR fit.


Compute Sufficient Statistics and Sparse LD
bed_xtx_xty() computes the marker-trait and phenotype cross-products used by the CSR model. The important returned quantities include:

stats$wy, corresponding to marker-trait cross-products;
stats$ww, containing marker diagonal cross-products;
stats$yy, containing phenotype sums of squares;
metadata such as marker count, trait count, and sample size when available.

sparseLD_stream_CSR() then writes thresholded sparse LD from the same BED source. Its r2_threshold, distance limits, selected rows, allele frequencies, marker columns, and scaling assumptions should be reported. sparseLD_read_CSR() can inspect the resulting representation, but users should rely on package readers and writers rather than treating the on-disk files as a stable manual file-format API.


Fit and Compare the CSR Model
stblr_csr() combines stats with the CSR ld_prefix. A short call is:
fit_csr <- stblr_csr(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  n = Glist$n,
  nit = 1000,
  nburn = 100,
  seed = 10
)
Matched BED and CSR fits should agree qualitatively when marker order, selected rows, genotype scaling, priors, and MCMC settings match. Exact equality is not expected. Sparse-LD thresholding, residual representation, update scheduling, floating-point behavior, and Monte Carlo variation can all produce differences. Compare posterior effects, PIPs, and variance summaries; do not treat equality of individual draws as a validation target.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
Annotation-Model Comparison Workflow
annotation_based_models.R starts from the same BED-to-CSR preparation path, then compares annotation prior families while holding stats, sparse LD, and marker order fixed.
Its stages are:
mtsim_annotation()
    -> summarize_annotation_signal()
    -> bed_xtx_xty()
    -> sparseLD_stream_CSR()
    -> align annotation matrix A
    -> fit fixed, learned, group, and SBayesRC-style CSR models
    -> compact fit, marker, variance, and annotation summaries

Simulate and Inspect Annotation Signal
mtsim_annotation() simulates multi-trait phenotypes, marker effects, overlapping annotation memberships, enriched causal-marker sampling, and marker-specific prior values. It is useful because the annotation architecture and causal markers are known.
Before fitting, summarize_annotation_signal(sim) reports annotation size, causal-marker counts, and causal rates. These are truth-aware simulation diagnostics. They are unavailable in real data, where causal membership is not known.


Prepare Shared CSR Inputs and Align A
The workflow computes sufficient statistics and streams sparse LD exactly as in the plain CSR workflow. It then constructs an (m K) annotation matrix A, where rows are markers and columns are annotations.
rownames(A) <- marker_id
stopifnot(nrow(A) == length(cls), identical(rownames(A), marker_id))
The alignment check is essential. Row (i) of A must describe the same marker as row (i) of stats$wy, stats$ww, the sparse-LD rows and columns, and the returned marker-level posterior summaries.


Fit Four Annotation Prior Families
The script fits:

stblr_csr_prior_annot() with fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities and variance multipliers;
stblr_csr_learn_annot() with annotation effects learned during fitting;
stblr_csr_group_annot() with mutually exclusive group-level priors;
stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic() with an SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior.

The fourth model uses annotation-dependent probit stick-breaking probabilities over an exact null and multiple active variance components. It is not an exact reproduction of the published GCTB SBayesRC implementation as exposed by default: sblr uses a CSR sparse-LD likelihood and defaults to gamma = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1). Users who want the published gamma grid can supply:
gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
Matching that grid aligns one part of the prior specification; it does not make the complete implementation identical to GCTB SBayesRC. See Annotation-informed models for the model comparison.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
Fit Object Structure
The public wrappers format native sampler results into named lists. Always inspect names(fit) and the relevant help page because some components are model-specific or optional.







Component
Interpretation




bm
Posterior mean marker effects, usually an (m n_t) matrix.


dm
Posterior inclusion probabilities or inclusion summaries, usually aligned with bm.


b
Current or returned marker-effect state, when returned. It is not the same as bm.


r
Current or returned marker-scale residual state, when returned.


vbs
MCMC trace of marker-effect variance scale.


vgs
MCMC trace of genetic variance summaries.


ves
MCMC trace of residual variance summaries.


covb
Posterior marker-effect covariance summary, when returned.


covg
Posterior genetic covariance summary, when returned.


cove
Posterior residual covariance summary, when returned.


pi
Final or current inclusion-probability summary, with exact meaning determined by the wrapper.


pim
Posterior mean inclusion-probability summary, when returned.


input
Resolved model inputs, preprocessing choices, priors, and MCMC settings added by public wrappers.



Some fits additionally return correlation versions rb, rg, and re when the corresponding covariance matrices are valid. CSR fits may also return vle and vld, separating linkage-equilibrium and LD contributions under the sampler’s definitions.

Annotation-Specific Components

Learned-annotation fits return eta_pi and eta_vb, summarizing annotation effects on inclusion probabilities and variance multipliers.
Group fits return group_pi, group_vb_multiplier, group_nincluded, and group_size.
SBayesRC-style fits return alpha, sigmaSqAlpha, comp_prob, and ncomp. Here alpha contains annotation coefficients for stick-breaking steps, sigmaSqAlpha summarizes their variance parameters, comp_prob contains marker-level posterior component probabilities, and ncomp summarizes numbers of markers assigned to components.

These components have different dimensions and meanings. Do not compare an eta_pi coefficient directly with an alpha coefficient without accounting for their distinct links and prior structures.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
Compact Reporting
Marker-level matrices can contain tens of thousands or millions of entries. Printing fit$bm, fit$dm, fit$b, a full comp_prob, or the complete fit object floods the console and obscures useful diagnostics. Full objects should remain available for analysis and serialization, while routine reporting should aggregate them deliberately.
A compact trait-level summary can include:

number of markers and traits;
sum of PIPs by trait, colSums(fit$dm);
mean absolute posterior effect, colMeans(abs(fit$bm));
means and selected quantiles of vbs, vgs, and ves;
compact diagonal and off-diagonal covariance summaries when present.

For example:
data.frame(
  trait = colnames(fit$dm),
  pip_sum = colSums(fit$dm),
  mean_abs_bm = colMeans(abs(fit$bm)),
  mean_vg = colMeans(fit$vgs),
  mean_ve = colMeans(fit$ves)
)
Treat sum(PIP) as an effective posterior number of included markers under the fitted model, not as a known count of causal variants.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
PIPs and Top-Marker Summaries
For marker (i) and trait (t), dm[i, t] estimates posterior evidence that the marker is active under the fitted likelihood, prior, and sampler. A useful top-marker table contains marker identifier, trait, PIP, absolute posterior mean effect, and signed posterior mean effect:
ord <- order(-fit$dm[, 1], -abs(fit$bm[, 1]))
head(data.frame(
  marker = rownames(fit$dm),
  pip = fit$dm[, 1],
  abs_bm = abs(fit$bm[, 1]),
  bm = fit$bm[, 1]
)[ord, ], 10)
Rankings depend on LD, the marker set, priors, phenotype architecture, summary-statistic quality, and MCMC settings. Correlated markers can share posterior evidence, and an annotation-informed prior can change rankings even when the likelihood is unchanged. Top markers are candidates for follow-up, not automatically causal variants.
When comparing models, report whether the same markers, traits, LD, and MCMC settings were used. Differences in rankings otherwise combine model effects with input differences.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
Variance and Covariance Summaries
vgs and ves provide iteration-level genetic and residual variance summaries. vbs tracks the active marker-effect variance scale used by the model. Report posterior means together with quantiles or trace diagnostics, not only final values.
In simulations, compare posterior genetic and residual variance summaries with the generating architecture and requested h2. Do not expect exact recovery from a short chain or finite simulated data. Realized simulated heritability, sparse-LD approximation, prior shrinkage, and Monte Carlo variation all affect the comparison.
For multiple traits, covb, covg, and cove summarize different covariance targets when returned. Their off-diagonal entries should be interpreted only after confirming that the fitted wrapper actually represents the intended joint model. Parallel single-trait fits do not automatically become a fully joint multi-trait analysis.

title: Workflows and Outputs
text:
Annotation-Level Diagnostics
Annotation diagnostics answer different questions depending on whether truth is available and how annotation information enters the prior.

Simulation Truth and Posterior Summaries
For an mtsim_annotation() result:
summarize_annotation_signal(sim)
summarize_annotation_signal(sim, fit)
The first call summarizes true annotation sizes and causal enrichment. The second adds annotation-level mean PIP and mean absolute posterior effects for each trait. Comparing these tables helps assess recovery in simulations, but does not establish causal annotation effects in real data.


Learned and Group Annotation Fits
For learned models, inspect eta_pi and eta_vb together with posterior marker summaries, annotation prevalence, and correlations among annotation columns. Large coefficients can reflect true enrichment, overlap, collinearity, weak regularization, or short-chain instability.
For group models, report group sizes alongside group_pi, group_vb_multiplier, and group_nincluded. Small groups generally produce less stable group-level summaries.


SBayesRC-Style Prior-Architecture Diagnostics
The exported helpers convert SBayesRC-style annotation coefficients into component probabilities and expected gamma multipliers:

sbayesrc_annotation_pi() and sbayesrc_annotation_gamma_mean() summarize individual annotation coefficient rows;
sbayesrc_marker_pi() and sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean() combine complete marker annotation profiles with alpha.

Annotation-row summaries are not the same as marker-level predictions when annotations overlap. A compact report can show the annotation-level expected gamma table, summary() of marker expected gamma, and its correlation with PIP by trait. These describe the fitted prior architecture and posterior relationship; they are not proof that an annotation or marker is causal.
See Technical annotation priors and Technical SBayesRC-style annotations for the underlying prior structures.

title: Workflows and Outputs
Workflows and Outputs
text:
Recommended Reporting Checklist
For each reported fit, record:

Data source: BED source or summary-statistics provenance, selected chromosomes/regions, marker count, and marker-order checks.
Samples and traits: sample size n, selected sample rows, number of traits, phenotype preprocessing, and missingness handling.
LD construction: source panel, r2_threshold, distance limits, scaling, block settings, and CSR prefix provenance.
Model and priors: wrapper name, plain or annotation-informed prior, inclusion and variance-prior settings, annotation preprocessing, group definitions, and gamma grid where relevant.
MCMC settings: nit, nburn, nthin, chains, seed, scheduling choices, and thread count.
Convergence caveat: diagnostics performed and any limitations caused by short or single-chain runs.
Marker summaries: PIP sums, top-marker table, and selected posterior effect summaries without dumping full matrices.
Variance summaries: posterior means and uncertainty for genetic, residual, and active marker-effect variance quantities.
Annotation summaries: annotation size, enrichment or learned coefficients, group summaries, or SBayesRC-style component diagnostics when relevant.
Validation and sensitivity: BED-versus-CSR comparison, simulation truth, held-out prediction, prior sensitivity, and LD-threshold sensitivity as appropriate.

For annotation-informed analyses, explicitly state that enrichment and posterior prioritization are evidence structures rather than causal proof.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
This appendix defines the sparse linkage disequilibrium (LD) representation used by the current sblr BED-to-CSR workflow. It describes the statistical matrix, compressed sparse row (CSR) structure, disk-backed construction, indexing conventions, alignment requirements, and downstream conversion used by stblr_csr() and related wrappers.
The stable user-facing contract is deliberately narrower than the current binary-file implementation:
The present file suffixes, integer widths, floating-point widths, metadata keys, and upper-triangle storage convention are documented here to explain behavior and support validation. They should not be treated as a guaranteed manual file-format API. Use package readers, writers, and samplers rather than editing or independently constructing these files.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
section: From BED Genotypes to Sufficient Statistics and Sparse LD
text:
From BED Genotypes to Sufficient Statistics and Sparse LD
For genotype matrix (X), phenotype vector (y), and marker effects (b), a summary-statistics marker sampler needs quantities including
\[
wy=X^\top y,
\qquad
ww_i=x_i^\top x_i,
\qquad
yy=y^\top y,
\]
and enough off-diagonal marker information to update
\[
r=X^\top(y-Xb)=wy-X^\top Xb.
\]
In the BED-derived workflow, these inputs are prepared in two coordinated branches:
the same BED files + cls + rows + allele frequencies
    |
    +--> bed_xtx_xty() ------> stats$wy, stats$ww, stats$yy
    |
    +--> sparseLD_stream_CSR() ------> disk-backed sparse correlations
                                              |
                                              v
                              stblr_csr(stats, ld_prefix, ...)
bed_xtx_xty() supplies the phenotype cross-products and diagonal marker cross-products. sparseLD_stream_CSR() supplies retained off-diagonal marker correlations. During CSR model setup, the sampler combines the stored correlations with stats$ww to recover the corresponding off-diagonal cross-product scale.
This split is important: the on-disk values are correlations, not raw (X_i^X_j), and the diagonal cross-products are supplied separately by stats$ww.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
section: Matrix Represented by the Current Writer
text:
Matrix Represented by the Current Writer
The current BED sparse-LD writer standardizes each selected marker using its allele frequency, mean-imputes missing genotypes to zero on that standardized scale, computes marker cross-products, and normalizes off-diagonal entries to correlations:
\[
r_{ij}
=
\frac{x_i^\top x_j}
{\sqrt{(x_i^\top x_i)(x_j^\top x_j)}}.
\]
The writer retains an off-diagonal pair (i<j) when it passes the configured distance rules and
\[
r_{ij}^2 \geq \texttt{r2_threshold}.
\]
The stored value is signed (r_{ij}), not (r_{ij}^2). The current streamed artifact stores:

only the upper triangle, (j>i);
no explicit diagonal entries;
an implicit diagonal correlation of one; and
only pairs passing the threshold and window rules.

Thus the disk artifact is a sparse, upper-triangle, correlation-like representation of LD. It is not itself the complete (X^X) matrix.
When a CSR ST-BLR sampler opens the prefix, it reads the stored correlation and constructs a symmetric in-memory neighbor structure. For each retained pair it converts
\[
r_{ij}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\widetilde{X_i^\top X_j}
=
r_{ij}\sqrt{ww_iww_j}.
\]
The diagonal contribution remains ww[i]. This is why the sparse-LD prefix and sufficient statistics must use compatible samples, marker scaling, and marker order. The current shared-LD ST-BLR setup also requires compatible ww across trait columns.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
What CSR Means
Compressed sparse row format represents a sparse matrix without allocating all (m^2) entries. Three arrays describe the retained entries:







Array
Current conceptual role




row_ptr
Cumulative offsets delimiting each row’s retained entries; length (m+1).


col_idx
Column index for every retained entry; length nnz.


values
Value for every retained entry; length nnz.



For zero-based row pointers, entries belonging to row (i) occupy positions
\[
\texttt{row\_ptr}[i]
\quad\text{through}\quad
\texttt{row\_ptr}[i+1]-1.
\]
For example, consider the upper-triangle entries
row 0: (column 1, 0.40), (column 3, -0.20)
row 1: (column 3, 0.15)
row 2: no retained entries
row 3: no retained entries
Their CSR arrays are conceptually:
row_ptr = [0, 2, 3, 3, 3]
col_idx = [1, 3, 3]
values  = [0.40, -0.20, 0.15]
row_ptr is always a cumulative pointer array. The one_based option of sparseLD_read_CSR() converts returned column indices for convenient R inspection; it does not convert the row pointers.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
section: Why Disk-Backed Sparse CSR Is Used
text:
Why Disk-Backed Sparse CSR Is Used
A dense (mm) LD matrix requires (O(m^2)) storage. This becomes prohibitive for genome-scale marker sets even when most scientifically useful LD relationships are local or sufficiently strong.
Sparse CSR reduces storage toward (O(m+)), where nnz is the number of retained off-diagonal upper-triangle entries. Disk-backed storage provides two additional advantages:

the resulting LD artifact can be reused by multiple CSR model fits; and
the complete sparse arrays do not have to be returned to or retained in R during construction.

sparseLD_stream_CSR() processes marker blocks, computes candidate cross-products for block pairs, applies distance and (r^2) rules, and writes retained entries incrementally. It still needs working memory for decoded genotype blocks and block cross-products, but it avoids constructing either a dense whole-genome LD matrix or the complete sparse result in R.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Stable User-Facing Contract
The supported workflow treats the sparse-LD artifact as an opaque package- managed object identified by a prefix:
ld_prefix <- file.path(output_dir, "chr1_ld")

sparseLD_stream_CSR(
  bed_files = Glist$bedfiles[chr],
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = list(cls),
  out_prefix = ld_prefix,
  rows = NULL,
  af = list(Glist$af[[chr]][cls]),
  r2_threshold = 0.001,
  block_size = 1024,
  nthreads = 4
)
The stable usage expectations are:

all files belonging to a prefix are created and retained together;
sparseLD_read_CSR(ld_prefix) is used for inspection and validation;
stblr_csr(..., ld_prefix = ld_prefix) and related wrappers consume it;
marker order and construction settings are recorded externally; and
package functions handle file naming, binary types, index bases, diagonal convention, and conversion to sampler structures.

Analysis code should not assume that current suffixes, metadata keys, or binary encodings will remain unchanged. Independent tools that manually write these files depend on implementation details and can silently become incompatible after package changes.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
section: ld_prefix and the Current Disk Artifact
text:
ld_prefix and the Current Disk Artifact
ld_prefix is a common path prefix, not a single file and not an in-memory matrix. The current implementation derives several files from it. For example, a prefix path/chr1_ld currently identifies:
path/chr1_ld.row_ptr.u64.bin
path/chr1_ld.col_idx.u32.0based.bin
path/chr1_ld.values.f32.bin
path/chr1_ld.meta.txt
These names expose current implementation details:

row pointers are currently unsigned 64-bit integers;
column indices are currently unsigned 32-bit zero-based integers;
stored correlations are currently 32-bit floating-point values; and
metadata is currently a text file describing dimensions and settings.

The metadata currently records fields such as marker count, nnz, triangle and diagonal conventions, value type, normalization, threshold, distance limits, block size, thread count, and used sample count.
Treat the complete prefix as one artifact. Do not mix files from separate runs. Do not overwrite an important prefix when changing samples, marker sets, allele frequencies, distance windows, or thresholds. Prefer distinct, descriptive prefixes and retain construction provenance beside them.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Exported and Internal Helpers
Current NAMESPACE and wrapper status distinguish the supported public path from lower-level generated functions:








Helper
Current role
Current status




sparseLD_stream_CSR()
Computes BED-derived sparse LD and streams the disk-backed prefix.
Exported; principal user-facing constructor.


sparseLD_read_CSR()
Reads a written prefix into R for inspection and validation.
Exported; user-facing reader.


sparseLD_to_CSR()
Computes the same upper-triangle sparse representation and returns arrays in memory.
Generated lower-level wrapper; not exported in the current NAMESPACE.


sparseLD_write_CSR()
Delegates to sparseLD_stream_CSR() with an output prefix.
Generated alias/internal wrapper; not exported in the current NAMESPACE.



The lower-level wrappers can be useful during development, but they are not the documented model handoff. In particular, stblr_csr() accepts ld_prefix, not an R list returned by sparseLD_to_CSR().
The package also contains older or separate CSR conversion code for other LD inputs. Its conventions should not be assumed to be identical to the BED-streamed prefix described here.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Sparse-LD Construction Settings
Sparse-LD settings affect memory, runtime, disk use, and the statistical approximation. They should be selected deliberately and reported with model results.

Marker and Sample Selection

bed_files

Paths to one or more PLINK BED files. Their corresponding cls entries define the concatenated model-marker order.

n

Number of individuals encoded by the BED source.

cls

A list of marker-column index vectors, one per BED file. The order within and across these vectors becomes the sparse-LD row and column order.

rows

Optional positive one-based sample indices. When supplied, LD is computed from this selected sample. The same sample selection must underlie the sufficient statistics used downstream.

af

Optional list of allele frequencies aligned to cls. When omitted, the writer computes allele frequencies from the selected packed genotypes. Supplied values must be finite and in ([0,1]). Missing genotypes are represented as zero after standardization, corresponding to mean imputation on that scale.




Threshold and Window Settings

r2_threshold

Minimum squared correlation for retaining an eligible pair. The writer compares (r_{ij}^2) with this value but stores signed (r_{ij}). A larger threshold produces a sparser approximation and may remove weak but collectively relevant LD.

max_distance_variants

Maximum difference in model-order marker indices. Positive values restrict retained pairs to this index window. A value of zero disables this restriction in the current implementation.

max_distance_bp

Maximum base-pair separation when positions are supplied. Positive values restrict retained pairs by physical distance. A value of zero disables this restriction. The implementation evaluates forward position differences, so pos_bp should be aligned to marker order and ordered consistently within the intended genomic segments.

pos_bp

Optional list of marker base-pair positions aligned to cls. When absent, the base-pair distance restriction cannot be applied, even if max_distance_bp is positive.


A pair must pass every enabled window rule before its (r^2) is tested. Disabling both distance restrictions permits all upper-triangle marker pairs to be considered and can be computationally expensive.


Computational Settings

block_size

Number of markers decoded and compared in a working block. Larger values can improve matrix-multiplication efficiency but increase working memory roughly through genotype-block and block-cross-product buffers. It changes the construction strategy, not the intended retention rule.

nthreads

Requested OpenMP thread count. It affects construction performance and may affect low-level floating-point execution details, but it is not an LD threshold or model-prior parameter.




Scaling
sparseLD_stream_CSR() does not expose a scale argument. The current writer always constructs its correlation values from allele-frequency-standardized markers. By contrast, bed_xtx_xty() exposes scale. For the standard BED-to-CSR handoff, use compatible standardized marker statistics:
stats <- bed_xtx_xty(..., af = af, scale = TRUE)
sparseLD_stream_CSR(..., af = list(af))
Using bed_xtx_xty(..., scale = FALSE) with the current standardized correlation writer changes the scale relationship assumed when the sampler combines r_ij with stats$ww. Such combinations require explicit validation rather than being assumed compatible.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Index Bases and Diagonal Convention
Three conventions must be distinguished:

rows and cls supplied from R use the documented R-facing indexing expected by their wrappers.
Current on-disk col_idx entries are zero-based.
sparseLD_read_CSR(prefix, one_based = TRUE) returns one-based column indices for convenient R inspection.

The reader’s one_based argument changes only the returned col_idx vector. row_ptr remains a zero-based cumulative pointer array whose first value is zero and whose final value is nnz.
The current streamed artifact omits diagonal entries and reports diag = "implicit_1". Downstream ST-BLR samplers use the supplied stats$ww for diagonal (X_i^X_i) contributions. Users inspecting the sparse arrays should not mistake absence of explicit diagonal entries for a zero diagonal.
Package functions validate and handle these conventions. Manual index conversion or insertion of diagonal values risks corrupting the expected contract.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Marker-Order, Sample, and Scaling Invariants
Sparse arrays contain positional indices, not biological marker identifiers. The most important cross-layer invariant is:
Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls]
    == Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
    == rows of stats$wy and stats$ww
    == rows and columns of sparse LD
    == rows of an annotation matrix A
    == rows of fit$bm and fit$dm
Establish and retain marker order explicitly:
marker_id <- Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
cls <- match(marker_id, Glist$rsids[[chr]])

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(cls),
  identical(Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls], marker_id)
)
For multiple BED files, the concatenation of cls[[1]], cls[[2]], and so on defines the CSR order. Allele-frequency and position lists must follow the same per-file and concatenated order.
The same selected sample must underlie LD and sufficient statistics. If rows is used, apply it consistently. If allele frequencies are supplied, they must correspond to that construction and marker order. If annotations are later used, align their rows before fitting:
rownames(A) <- marker_id
stopifnot(identical(rownames(A), marker_id))
A permutation error can produce dimensionally valid CSR files and model fits while assigning LD or annotations to the wrong markers. Dimension checks alone cannot detect this error.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Reading and Validating a Prefix
Use the exported reader to inspect a prefix without manually decoding the binary files:
ld <- sparseLD_read_CSR(ld_prefix, one_based = TRUE)

stopifnot(
  ld$nrow == length(cls),
  ld$ncol == length(cls),
  length(ld$row_ptr) == length(cls) + 1L,
  length(ld$col_idx) == length(ld$values),
  tail(ld$row_ptr, 1) == length(ld$values),
  ld$index_base == 1,
  identical(ld$diag, "implicit_1")
)
The current reader checks that required metadata dimensions exist, reads the expected byte counts, verifies that row pointers begin at zero and end at nnz, requires nondecreasing row pointers, checks column-index bounds, and rejects non-finite values.
Additional analysis-level validation should confirm:

cls contains no missing marker matches.
LD dimensions equal the intended marker count.
row_ptr has length (m+1).
col_idx and values have equal length.
the final row pointer equals nnz.
returned index_base matches how col_idx is being inspected.
the upper-triangle and implicit-diagonal conventions are understood.
values are finite signed correlations and remain within plausible correlation bounds.
n_used, thresholds, windows, and marker count match the intended run.
stats$wy, every stats$ww vector, annotations, and posterior rows use exactly the same marker order.

The reader can validate structural properties but cannot prove that the BED source, allele frequencies, sample rows, phenotypes, annotations, or marker identities are scientifically aligned. Retain that provenance separately.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
How stblr_csr() Consumes the Prefix
The public model handoff is short:
fit <- stblr_csr(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  n = n,
  scheduled = FALSE
)
During setup, the current ST-BLR CSR implementation:

checks that metadata marker count matches the model marker count;
reads the zero-based upper-triangle arrays;
validates row pointers, column bounds, finite correlations, and positive stats$ww;
ignores any explicit self-pairs if encountered;
converts retained (r_{ij}) to (r_{ij}); and
creates a symmetric in-memory neighbor structure for residual updates.

For marker effect (b_i), the diagonal residual contribution uses (ww_i b_i), while retained off-diagonal neighbors use the converted cross-product values. Missing off-diagonal entries are treated as zero in the sparse approximation.
Annotation-aware CSR wrappers use the same LD prefix and marker-order contract. Their differences concern prior structure, not CSR construction.

title: Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR
text:
Scheduled Sparse Updates
stblr_csr(..., scheduled = TRUE) uses a scheduled marker-update implementation that can revisit likely null markers less frequently and wake retained LD neighbors after an effect change. Settings such as full_sweep_every, candidate_threshold, candidate_lifetime, null_skip_base, null_skip_max, and LD-neighbor wake-up controls affect the sampler’s computational schedule.
These controls are separate from CSR construction settings:

r2_threshold and distance windows determine which LD edges exist;
scheduling controls determine when markers and retained neighbors are reconsidered during MCMC.

Both can affect finite-run behavior and performance. The statistical prior is unchanged by choosing a scheduled path, but aggressive sparse scheduling must be checked for adequate mixing and sensitivity. See Single-trait models for the scheduling controls.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
This appendix develops the cross-trait phenotype and sample-overlap information required by multi-trait Bayesian linear regression (MTBLR) from summary statistics. It preserves the SSY and overlap derivations from the archived theory draft, connects them to the current sblr multi-trait interfaces, and distinguishes mathematically required quantities from current implementation constraints.
The central issue is simple: separate single-trait summary statistics preserve each trait’s marginal phenotype sum of squares, but they do not preserve cross-trait phenotype products. A joint model with residual covariance needs those cross-products or defensible approximations to them.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Multi-Trait Individual-Level Model
Let (T) denote the number of traits. For a fully overlapping sample, define:

(Y), an (nT) phenotype matrix;
(X), an (nm) genotype matrix;
(B), an (mT) marker-effect matrix; and
(E_Y), an (nT) residual matrix.

The multi-trait linear model is
[ Y=XB+E_Y. ]
For individual (i), the residual vector may be modeled as
[ e_iN_T(0,_e), ]
where (_e) is the residual covariance matrix. Marker-effect vectors may also share covariance. For example, an active marker-effect vector (b_j) may have a prior involving a covariance matrix (_b).
These two covariance structures have different meanings:

(_b) describes prior or posterior covariance among marker effects across traits and enables genetic information sharing;
(_e) describes covariance among residual phenotype deviations for individuals observed on the same traits.

Residual covariance is therefore directly tied to which individuals are shared across traits.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
section: Why Marginal Trait Statistics Are Not Enough
text:
Why Marginal Trait Statistics Are Not Enough
For one trait (t), the phenotype-side scalar summary is
[ yy_t=y_ty_t=i y{it}2. ]
Together with (X^y_t), genotype cross-products, and (n_t), this can support a single-trait likelihood. Repeating those inputs for several traits supports separate or parallel single-trait fits.
A joint multi-trait likelihood additionally depends on cross-trait phenotype products:
[ y_t^y_s = i y{it}y_{is}. ]
The marginal values (yy_t) and (yy_s) do not determine this cross-product. For example, two phenotype pairs can have identical marginal sums of squares but opposite cross-trait correlations.
Consequently, a full residual covariance update cannot be reconstructed from trait-specific yy values alone. It requires the complete cross-trait phenotype cross-product matrix, usually denoted SSY or (Y^Y), together with a clear sample-overlap interpretation.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Multi-Trait Summary Statistics
Under full sample overlap with one common (X), the central summary statistics are:
[ WY=X^Y, XX=X^X, SSY=Y^Y, n. ]
Their dimensions are:








Quantity
Dimension
Meaning




(WY=X^Y)
(mT)
Marker-trait cross-products


(XX=X^X)
(mm)
Marker cross-products or compatible LD representation


(SSY=Y^Y)
(TT)
Trait cross-products


(n)
scalar
Number of jointly observed individuals



For partially overlapping studies, the representation expands to include:

trait-specific sample sizes (n_t);
pairwise overlap counts (N_{ts}); and
trait-pair-specific interpretations of cross-products.

Define the sample-overlap matrix
[ N=
\[\begin{bmatrix}
N_{11} & \cdots & N_{1T}\\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
N_{T1} & \cdots & N_{TT}
\end{bmatrix}\]
, ]
where
[ N_{ts} = |I_{ts}| ]
and (I_{ts}) is the set of individuals observed for both traits (t) and (s). By definition,
[ N_{tt}=n_t. ]

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Cross-Trait SSY
For partially overlapping traits, define
[ SSY_{ts} = {iI{ts}}y_{it}y_{is}. ]
The diagonal entries reduce to ordinary single-trait sums of squares:
[ SSY_{tt}=yy_t. ]
When all traits are observed on exactly the same individuals, (I_{ts}) is the common sample for every pair and
[ SSY=Y^Y ]
has its ordinary matrix-cross-product meaning.
When samples overlap only partially, SSY remains a useful symmetric matrix of pairwise cross-products, but its entries are calculated from different sets of individuals. It should not be interpreted as the cross-product of one complete rectangular phenotype matrix unless such a matrix actually exists.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Full Sample Overlap
The cleanest MTBLR setting has all traits measured on the same (n) individuals:
[ n_t=n, N_{ts}=n t,s. ]
Then:
[ WY=X^Y, SSY=Y^Y ]
can be computed directly, and the residual covariance has the conventional interpretation:
[ _e = (e_i) ]
for residual vectors observed jointly on the same individuals.
The current CSR MTBLR kernel is closest to this setting. It uses shared LD, requires equal trait sample sizes and matching ww values across traits, and accepts a full trait cross-product matrix through its yy argument.
The archived theory draft also defines a weaker “full-overlap” approximation for unequal marginal sample sizes:
[ N^{}_{ts} = (n_t,n_s). ]
This assumes the smaller study is nested within the larger study for each trait pair. It is useful as an explicit approximation, but it is not equivalent to all traits being measured on one common sample.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Partial Sample Overlap
With partial overlap, different trait pairs may share different individuals:
[ 0<N_{ts}<(n_t,n_s). ]
A convenient parameterization uses overlap fractions (p_{ts}):
[ N^{}{ts} = p{ts}(n_t,n_s), N_{tt}=n_t. ]
The matrix (N) records the amount of direct information available about each trait pair. A cross-trait phenotype covariance estimated from 500 shared individuals is not supported by the same information as one estimated from 50,000 shared individuals, even when the numerical correlation is identical.
Partial overlap complicates the likelihood because:

SSY entries arise from different pair-specific samples;
marker-trait statistics (X_t^y_t) may arise from different genotype samples;
LD and diagonal genotype cross-products may differ by trait;
residual covariance reflects only shared individuals; and
a single common (X^X) may not exactly represent every trait pair.

These issues require explicit modeling assumptions. Supplying an overlap matrix does not by itself make a shared-LD likelihood exact.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
No Overlap and Unknown Overlap
If traits (t) and (s) have no shared individuals,
[ N_{ts}=0. ]
There is then no direct individual-level cross-product (i y{it}y_{is}) for that pair. Setting
[ SSY_{ts}=0 ]
records the absence of observed cross-trait phenotype product under a centered phenotype convention. It does not establish that biological, genetic, or population-level residual correlation is zero.
Genetic covariance can still be informed by shared markers, aligned marker-trait associations, and an appropriate cross-study model. Residual covariance between non-overlapping samples, however, is not directly identified by observed paired residuals. It must be fixed, strongly regularized, inferred from external information, or excluded from the model.
When overlap is unknown, off-diagonal SSY is also unknown. Treating unknown overlap as full overlap can create spurious residual covariance; treating it as zero can discard real correlated-error information. Sensitivity analyses over plausible overlap assumptions are preferable to silently choosing either extreme.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
section: Phenotypic Variance From Marginal Summary Statistics
text:
Phenotypic Variance From Marginal Summary Statistics
For trait (t), let:
[ yy_t={iI_t}y{it}^2, n_t=|I_t|. ]
If phenotypes are centered or approximately centered, an empirical variance estimate is
[ (y_t) . ]
Using (n_t-1) instead gives the usual sample-variance denominator. The choice must match the intended likelihood and preprocessing convention. The archived reconstruction uses (yy_t/n_t) as the cross-product-per-observation quantity.
Collect the marginal variance estimates in:
[ _y^2 = ( , , ). ]
If phenotypes are not centered, (yy_t/n_t) is a second raw moment rather than a variance. Covariance reconstruction then requires explicit treatment of trait means.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Covariance Reconstruction From Correlations
Suppose a phenotypic correlation matrix
[ R_y=[r_{ts}] ]
is available from individual-level data, a reported study estimate, or an external source. Convert it to phenotype covariance units using:
[ {ts} = r{ts} . ]
In matrix form:
[ (Y) = D_yR_yD_y, ]
where
[ D_y = ( , , ). ]
This rescaling is essential. A correlation matrix alone is dimensionless and cannot replace phenotype cross-products when traits have different scales.
The supplied (R_y) must have the same trait order as yy, (n), (WY), and all covariance priors. If (R_y) comes from another sample, its transportability is an additional assumption.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Reconstructing SSY
Under the approximation that pairwise covariance is homogeneous across individuals and that missingness or study membership does not alter it,
[ E(y_{it}y_{is}) = _{ts} ]
for centered traits observed together. Therefore:
[
\[\begin{aligned}
E(SSY_{ts})
&=
E\left[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{ts}}y_{it}y_{is}
\right]\\
&=
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{ts}}E(y_{it}y_{is})\\
&=
N_{ts}\sigma_{ts}.
\end{aligned}\]
]
Replacing (_{ts}) with its estimate gives:
[ {ts} = N{ts}_{ts}. ]
In matrix notation:
[ = N(Y), ]
where () denotes elementwise multiplication.
The diagonal should be forced to the observed marginal sums of squares:
[ _{tt}=yy_t. ]
This avoids small inconsistencies caused by rounding, denominator choices, or correlation-matrix construction.
A short illustrative construction is:
vy <- yy / n
cov_y <- diag(sqrt(vy)) %*% R_y %*% diag(sqrt(vy))
SSY <- Nmat * cov_y
diag(SSY) <- yy
This is a reconstruction under assumptions, not an observed cross-product unless the input covariance and overlap information were obtained directly from the relevant individuals.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
First-Principles Assumptions
The reconstruction
[ {ts}=N{ts}_{ts} ]
rests on several assumptions.

Centered phenotypes
For nonzero means:
[ E(y_ty_s) = (y_t,y_s) +E(y_t)E(y_s). ]
The covariance-only reconstruction is therefore appropriate when phenotypes are centered, residualized with an intercept, or otherwise have negligible means on the relevant sample.


Random or ignorable missingness
The shared individuals (I_{ts}) should not have a systematically different cross-trait covariance from the target population. If overlap is selected by disease status, cohort, measurement protocol, or other trait-related factors, covariance homogeneity may fail.


Homogeneous covariance
The derivation assumes:
[ (y_{it},y_{is}) = _{ts} ]
for individuals contributing to the pairwise product. Cohort heterogeneity, ancestry differences, environmental strata, and phenotype harmonization can violate this assumption.


Correct overlap counts
The approximation uses the actual or defensible effective value of (N_{ts}). Rounding overlap fractions, using total study size instead of shared size, or ignoring duplicated participants changes the implied cross-product.


Compatible phenotype covariance
The correlation or covariance estimate must refer to phenotypes on compatible scales, with compatible covariate adjustment and trait definitions.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
section: Why SSY Matters for Residual Covariance
text:
Why SSY Matters for Residual Covariance
Let:
[ R_Y=Y-XB ]
be the individual-level residual matrix. Its cross-product is:
[
\[\begin{aligned}
R_Y^\top R_Y
&=
(Y-XB)^\top(Y-XB)\\
&=
Y^\top Y
-Y^\top XB
-B^\top X^\top Y
+B^\top X^\top XB.
\end{aligned}\]
]
Using summary-statistic notation:
[ R_Y^R_Y = SSY -WY^B -B^WY +B^XXB. ]
The off-diagonal entries of this residual cross-product depend directly on the off-diagonal entries of SSY. Without them, a sampler cannot reconstruct the full residual cross-product from marginal summaries alone.
The current CSR MTBLR implementation accepts a full (TT) matrix through its yy/YY argument. It combines that matrix with marker-trait cross-products, current effects, and marker-scale residual scores, then symmetrizes the resulting residual cross-product before updating the residual covariance matrix.
If only diagonal yy values are available, a model can still update trait-specific residual variances. A full residual covariance update then requires off-diagonal values to be fixed, reconstructed, externally supplied, or excluded.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Genetic Covariance and Residual Covariance
Multi-trait models can borrow information through both marker-effect and residual covariance, but these sources must not be conflated.

Marker-effect covariance
For marker (j), let:
[ b_j=
\[\begin{bmatrix}
b_{j1} & \cdots & b_{jT}
\end{bmatrix}\]
^. ]
A multi-trait prior can assign:
[ b_j N_T(0,_b) ]
on the active traits. Off-diagonal entries of (_b) allow effects to co-vary across traits. Trait-sharing model indicators can additionally encode whether a marker is active for specific subsets of traits.


Genetic covariance from fitted effects
With a common genotype matrix:
[ G_X=XB ]
has cross-product:
[ G_XG_X=BXXB. ]
Using marker-score residuals (R= WY-XXB), a symmetric summary-statistic estimate for traits (t) and (s) is:
[ G_{ts} = . ]
This quantity concerns genetic values induced by marker effects and LD. It is not determined by SSY alone.


Residual covariance
Residual covariance concerns phenotype variation not represented by the current marker effects. Its observed cross-trait information comes from shared individuals and therefore depends on SSY and sample overlap. A genetic correlation may exist with no sample overlap; direct residual covariance information cannot.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Simulation as a Known-Truth Check
mtsim() and mtsim_annotation() simulate all traits on one common genotype matrix and one common individual set. They generate:

marker-effect matrix B;
genetic values G;
residual matrix E;
phenotype matrix y;
target and observed genetic correlations; and
target and observed residual correlations.

For such simulations, full-overlap quantities can be calculated directly:
Y <- as.matrix(sim$y)
SSY <- crossprod(Y)
Nmat <- matrix(nrow(Y), nrow = ncol(Y), ncol = ncol(Y))
These simulations are useful for checking whether an MTBLR implementation recovers known covariance and sharing patterns. They do not validate partial-overlap reconstruction assumptions unless missingness or study separation is explicitly simulated.
The existing workflow scripts currently use the simulated phenotype columns primarily in parallel single-trait CSR and annotation-aware fits. A complete joint MTBLR workflow must additionally construct and validate full cross-trait inputs.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Practical Data Requirements
A joint summary-statistics MTBLR analysis should retain:







Object
Required contract




Trait names/order
Identical across every trait-indexed object


(WY=X^Y)
(mT), with marker and trait order recorded


ww / diagonal (XX)
Length (m) per trait; compatible with LD scaling


LD / (XX)
Marker order identical to rows of (WY)


SSY
Symmetric (TT) observed or reconstructed trait cross-product matrix


(n)
Trait-specific sample-size vector, even when all values are equal


Nmat
Symmetric (TT) pairwise overlap matrix used to justify SSY


Phenotype scaling
Centering, variance scaling, transformations, and covariate adjustment


Covariance priors
Trait order and units matching SSY and marker statistics



For current CSR MTBLR use, additionally verify that the shared-LD and equal sample-size restrictions are satisfied.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Validation Checks
Before fitting or interpreting a joint multi-trait model:

Confirm that SSY is (TT), finite, and symmetric.
Confirm that diag(SSY) equals the trait-specific yy values.
Check that observed full-overlap SSY = crossprod(Y) is positive semidefinite up to numerical tolerance.
For reconstructed pairwise SSY, inspect eigenvalues and understand that pairwise-valid entries do not automatically guarantee a globally positive semidefinite matrix.
Confirm that Nmat is symmetric and finite.
Confirm that:
[ N_{tt}=n_t ]
and:
[ 0N_{ts}(n_t,n_s). ]
Confirm that trait order is identical across SSY, Nmat, (WY), (n), (_b), (_e), prior scale matrices, and outputs.
Confirm that (WY), ww, and LD use the same marker order and compatible genotype scaling.
Confirm that reported phenotype correlations are on compatible phenotype definitions and scales.
Record whether every off-diagonal SSY value was observed, reconstructed, fixed, or assumed.
For current CSR MTBLR, confirm equal n values and equal ww vectors across traits.
Inspect covariance traces, eigenvalues, correlations, and sensitivity to overlap assumptions.

Positive semidefiniteness is especially important because covariance updates require valid scale matrices. Small negative eigenvalues may arise from rounding and can sometimes be regularized; substantial negative eigenvalues usually indicate incompatible pairwise inputs or assumptions.

title: Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Sample Overlap
text:
Limitations and Sensitivity Analysis
Multi-trait summary-statistics inference is sensitive to assumptions that are unnecessary or directly observable with complete individual-level data.

Overlap uncertainty: errors in (N_{ts}) directly alter reconstructed SSY off-diagonals.
Nonrandom missingness: shared individuals may not represent the marginal trait samples.
Phenotype heterogeneity: correlations can differ across cohorts, ancestries, environments, or phenotype definitions.
LD mismatch: trait-specific association statistics may not be compatible with one shared LD reference.
Scale mismatch: correlations, yy, (WY), and covariance priors may be expressed on different phenotype scales.
Weak identification: residual covariance is weakly or not directly identified when overlap is small, zero, or unknown.
Covariance instability: high-dimensional or highly correlated trait covariance matrices can be numerically unstable.
Current implementation scope: the CSR MTBLR kernel’s shared-LD and equal-(n) requirements are narrower than the most general partial-overlap theory.

Production analyses should compare plausible overlap matrices, phenotype correlation sources, residual covariance restrictions, and LD references. Repeated chains, covariance diagnostics, predictive validation, and sensitivity to regularization are required before interpreting cross-trait borrowing or covariance estimates.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
text:
This note describes the practical bridge from individual-level PLINK BED genotypes and aligned phenotypes to a disk-backed sparse-LD representation and the sufficient statistics required by stblr_csr(). The same starting data can also be fitted directly with stblr_bed_marker(), making the workflow useful for understanding and checking the relationship between the individual-level and summary-statistics paths.
The examples below are intentionally short. The complete executable sequence is in the sparse-LD/BED workflow. Its fitting steps are computationally expensive and its MCMC settings are demonstration settings rather than recommendations for real analysis.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: One Genotype Source, Two Fitting Paths
text:
One Genotype Source, Two Fitting Paths
The workflow begins with PLINK BED files, marker metadata, and one or more phenotypes. It then branches into two model-input representations:
BED files + phenotype y
        |
        v
align markers with cls and select sample rows
        |
        +--> bed_xtx_xty()
        |       |
        |       v
        |    stats$wy, stats$ww, stats$yy, n
        |
        +--> sparseLD_stream_CSR()
                |
                v
             ld_prefix
                |
                +--> sparseLD_read_CSR() for inspection
                |
                v
             stblr_csr()
                |
                v
          CSR posterior summaries

BED files + phenotype y + the same cls/rows/scaling
        |
        v
stblr_bed_marker()
        |
        v
optional BED-versus-CSR posterior comparison
The CSR path converts individual-level data into reusable cross-products and sparse LD files. The direct BED path retains access to observed genotypes during sampling. Both paths represent related marker-update calculations, but they are not numerically identical by construction.
The statistical role of each representation is developed in Data representations. This note focuses on object handoffs and practical contracts.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Selecting Samples and Markers From a BED-Backed Glist
text:
Selecting Samples and Markers From a BED-Backed Glist
A qgg Glist connects biological marker identities to BED file columns and allele frequencies. The principal objects are:







Object
Practical role




bed_files
Paths to one or more PLINK BED files containing individual-level genotypes.


n
Number of individuals encoded in the BED files.


Glist$rsids[[chr]]
Marker identities in BED column order for a chromosome.


Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
Selected marker identities in the intended LD/model order.


cls
BED column indices that map the intended LD/model order into Glist$rsids.


rows
Optional 1-based BED row indices selecting individuals.


af
Allele frequencies corresponding exactly to cls, used for genotype scaling.


y
Phenotype vector or matrix aligned to all individuals or to rows.



The workflow establishes marker order with:
chr <- 1
marker_id <- Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
cls <- match(marker_id, Glist$rsids[[chr]])
stopifnot(!anyNA(cls))

bed_files <- Glist$bedfiles[chr]
af <- Glist$af[[chr]][cls]
cls[j] identifies the BED column containing marker_id[j]. Its order, not just its set of values, determines the order of every downstream marker-indexed object.
For one BED file, bed_xtx_xty() receives cls as an integer vector. The sparse-LD helpers accept bed_files and cls as parallel collections, so cls is supplied as list(cls). For multiple BED files, each cls[[k]] selects and orders markers from bed_files[k]; the concatenated selection is the model order.
n is the total number of BED rows. If rows = NULL, all BED rows are used and y should have n rows. If rows is supplied, it selects the individuals used to construct statistics and LD, and y must describe that same selected sample in the expected order. The same rows value must be used for both branches of CSR preparation.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
text:
Simulating or Supplying Aligned Phenotypes
The workflow example simulates traits for Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]] and then scales the resulting phenotype matrix:
sim <- mtsim(Glist = Glist, chr = chr, rsids = marker_id, nt = 3, seed = 1)
y <- as.matrix(scale(sim$y))
Real analyses can replace this with observed phenotypes, but alignment and preprocessing must be explicit:

rows of y must correspond to BED individuals or the selected rows;
columns of y define traits and should have stable names;
centering and scaling choices affect stats$yy and prior initialization;
missing phenotype handling must be consistent with the chosen sample.

For trait (t), bed_xtx_xty() constructs quantities including
\[
wy_t = X^\top y_t,
\qquad
ww_t = \operatorname{diag}(X^\top X),
\qquad
yy_t = y_t^\top y_t.
\]
The sparse-LD branch must use the same version of (X), including sample rows and marker scaling, that generated these statistics.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Path A: Direct Individual-Level Fitting With stblr_bed_marker()
text:
Path A: Direct Individual-Level Fitting With stblr_bed_marker()
Use stblr_bed_marker() when individual-level BED genotypes and aligned phenotypes remain available during fitting and a separate sparse-LD artifact is not required. The sampler reads selected genotype blocks from BED and uses observed marker values directly.
fit_bed <- stblr_bed_marker(
  Glist = Glist,
  y = y,
  chr = chr,
  cls = cls,
  scale = TRUE,
  rows = NULL,
  pi_marker = 0.001,
  h2 = 0.5,
  nit = 1000,
  nburn = 100,
  seed = 10,
  scheduled = TRUE
)
This path is appropriate when:

individual-level data access is allowed throughout analysis;
reading BED blocks during sampling is acceptable;
observed genotype information is preferred to a thresholded LD approximation;
the fit is being used as a reference for CSR preparation or model behavior.

stblr_bed_marker() derives BED paths, allele frequencies, and marker names from Glist. If cls is omitted, the wrapper matches Glist$rsidsLD against Glist$rsids; supplying cls explicitly makes the comparison contract visible.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Path B, Step 1: Deriving wy, ww, and yy With bed_xtx_xty()
text:
Path B, Step 1: Deriving wy, ww, and yy With bed_xtx_xty()
bed_xtx_xty() converts the selected BED genotypes and phenotype matrix into sufficient statistics for ST-BLR fitting:
stats <- bed_xtx_xty(
  bed_file = bed_files,
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = cls,
  af = af,
  y = y,
  rows = NULL,
  scale = TRUE,
  nthreads = 4
)
The main output handoff is:







Object
Meaning and use




stats$wy
Marker-trait cross-products (X^Y); drives marker-residual scores.


stats$ww
Per-marker diagonal genotype cross-products; used by marker updates.


stats$yy
Per-trait phenotype sums of squares (y_t^y_t); used for likelihood and variance initialization.


stats$n
Sample size when returned; otherwise supply compatible n to stblr_csr().


stats$m
Marker count when returned; otherwise inferred from stats$ww[[1]].



stats$wy and stats$ww must each describe the same (m) markers, in the same order later used by the CSR LD matrix. stats$yy has one entry per trait, not one entry per marker.
bed_xtx_xty() accepts a single BED file path and a single cls vector. Current multi-file sparse-LD preparation therefore needs statistics assembled with a compatible marker order and sample definition; the clean workflow uses one chromosome and one BED file.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Path B, Step 2: Streaming Sparse LD With sparseLD_stream_CSR()
text:
Path B, Step 2: Streaming Sparse LD With sparseLD_stream_CSR()
sparseLD_stream_CSR() computes marker correlations from BED data, applies distance and (r^2) retention rules, and writes a disk-backed CSR representation:
ld_prefix <- file.path(output_dir, "chr1_ld")

ld_written <- sparseLD_stream_CSR(
  bed_files = bed_files,
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = list(cls),
  out_prefix = ld_prefix,
  rows = NULL,
  af = list(af),
  r2_threshold = 0.001,
  max_distance_bp = 0,
  max_distance_variants = 0,
  block_size = 1024,
  nthreads = 4
)
ld_prefix is not a matrix object. It is the common prefix for the metadata, row-pointer, column-index, and value files consumed by stblr_csr(). The writer returns a compact summary containing file paths, dimensions, the number of stored nonzero entries, construction settings, and sample counts.
Conceptually, CSR stores:

row_ptr: offsets delimiting retained entries for each LD row;
col_idx: column indices of retained marker pairs;
values: retained marker correlations (r).

The disk format stores the upper triangle with an implicit unit diagonal and zero-based column indices. Package functions handle this storage contract; analysis code should not manually alter index bases or binary files.
r2_threshold controls which correlations are retained by squared magnitude. The distance arguments can additionally restrict candidate marker pairs. Values of zero disable the corresponding distance restriction in the example workflow. These settings change the LD approximation and should be recorded with analysis outputs.

Related Sparse-LD Helpers
The package source currently contains four related Rcpp wrappers:








Helper
Behavior
Current package status




sparseLD_stream_CSR()
Computes sparse LD and writes the disk-backed CSR files at out_prefix, returning a writing summary.
Exported and used by the public workflow.


sparseLD_to_CSR()
Computes the sparse LD representation and returns row_ptr, col_idx, and values in an in-memory R list.
Generated internal wrapper; not currently exported or separately documented.


sparseLD_write_CSR()
Currently delegates to sparseLD_stream_CSR() and writes the same disk-backed representation.
Generated internal wrapper; not currently exported or separately documented.


sparseLD_read_CSR()
Reads an existing disk-backed CSR prefix into an R list for inspection.
Exported.



Use sparseLD_stream_CSR() for the supported BED-to-disk workflow. The in-memory sparseLD_to_CSR() representation can be useful during development, but it materializes sparse arrays in R and is not the input contract used by stblr_csr(). The sparseLD_write_CSR() alias should not be treated as a separate stable public API while it remains unexported.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Path B, Step 3: Fitting Summary-Statistics BLR With stblr_csr()
text:
Path B, Step 3: Fitting Summary-Statistics BLR With stblr_csr()
stblr_csr() combines the sufficient-statistics object with the disk-backed LD prefix:
fit_csr <- stblr_csr(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  n = Glist$n,
  pi_marker = 0.001,
  h2 = 0.5,
  nit = 1000,
  nburn = 100,
  seed = 10,
  scheduled = FALSE
)
Its core data handoff is:
n + stats$yy
    -> phenotype variance and prior initialization

stats$wy + stats$ww + ld_prefix
    -> marker-update and residual-score calculations
The wrapper infers the number of traits from length(stats$yy). It takes n from the function argument or stats$n, and takes (m) from the function argument, stats$m, or length(stats$ww[[1]]). Explicitly supplying n and checking (m) before fitting makes the data contract easier to audit.
stats$wy, stats$ww, and stats$yy summarize the phenotype side and diagonal marker information. The files at ld_prefix provide the retained off-diagonal marker relationships needed to update residual scores after marker effects change. The summary-statistics path therefore depends on both objects; neither is sufficient by itself.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
section: Marker Order, Allele Frequency, Scaling, Rows, and LD Thresholds
text:
Marker Order, Allele Frequency, Scaling, Rows, and LD Thresholds
The central practical invariant is:
Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls]
    == Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
    == rows of stats$wy and stats$ww
    == rows and columns of sparse LD
    == rows of any later annotation matrix
    == rows of fit$bm and fit$dm
The first equality should be tested directly:
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(cls),
  identical(Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls], Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]])
)
The remaining equalities are positional contracts. Sparse LD binary files do not supply biological marker IDs to repair a mismatch later. Retain marker_id <- Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]] beside the preparation outputs and attach or verify it whenever annotations and posterior summaries are joined.
Scaling also has to match. If bed_xtx_xty(..., scale = TRUE) standardizes markers using af, then sparse LD must be constructed from the same selected samples and corresponding allele frequencies. If rows is used, use it in both calls and ensure y describes those rows. LD thresholds and distance limits should be treated as recorded model-input settings, not merely performance options.
The annotation workflow extends this contract with:
rownames(A) <- marker_id
stopifnot(nrow(A) == length(cls), identical(rownames(A), marker_id))
This is the handoff from the base CSR workflow to the models described in Annotation-informed models.

title: Sparse-LD and BED Workflows
text:
Validation Checklist
Before fitting stblr_csr(), verify:

cls has no missing values.
Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls] exactly matches Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]].
y has n rows when rows = NULL, or describes the selected rows when rows is supplied.
af has one value per selected marker and follows cls order.
Every trait’s stats$wy and stats$ww has length (m=).
stats$yy has one value per phenotype trait.
CSR nrow and ncol both equal (m), and row_ptr has length (m+1).
CSR index bases are left to package functions; use one_based only when inspecting a returned R object.
CSR metadata records the expected sample count, threshold, and distance settings.
Annotation rows and marker/group vectors match marker_id exactly before annotation-informed models are fitted.
Posterior rows are interpreted in the same marker order.
Real analyses use adequate chains, convergence checks, and posterior predictive diagnostics.
