title: Multi-Trait Models
text: Multi-trait Bayesian linear regression (MT-BLR) models several traits jointly so that evidence can be shared through marker-effect patterns and covariance structures. This note introduces the main model ideas and explains how they relate to the current sblr implementation. The deeper requirements for cross-trait summary statistics and sample overlap are covered in Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Overlap.

title: Multi-Trait Models
Multi-Trait Models
Multi-Trait Models
text:
Marker Effects, Sharing, and Pleiotropy
A multi-trait marker model needs to distinguish between two related ideas:

Trait-sharing pattern: which elements of (_i) are active.
Effect covariance: how the non-zero effects vary together across traits.

For three traits, example sharing patterns are:



Pattern
Interpretation




000
Marker is inactive for all traits


100
Marker is active only for trait 1


110
Marker is active for traits 1 and 2


111
Marker is active for all three traits



The model can assign prior probabilities to these patterns and update their posterior support. A shared active pattern is compatible with pleiotropy, but it is not proof that one marker is the biological cause of multiple traits. LD, prior assumptions, trait scaling, and the available summary statistics also influence the inferred sharing pattern.

title: Multi-Trait Models
text:
Multi-Trait Sparse Priors
The single-trait sparse prior combines an exact null component with an active normal component. MT-BLR generalizes this idea by assigning each marker a trait-sharing model (s_i). Conditional on (s_i), inactive effects are fixed at zero and active effects are drawn from a multivariate distribution.
A schematic prior is
[ s_i (), ]
[ {i,s_i} s_i ( , {b,s_i} ), ]
where () contains prior probabilities for the allowed sharing patterns and (_{b,s_i}) is the active-effect covariance submatrix for pattern (s_i).
The allowed model space is an important modeling decision:

A full model space permits all (2^t) inactive/active patterns.
A restrictive model space may permit only all-null and all-active patterns.
Custom prior probabilities can favor trait-specific or broadly shared effects.

As the number of traits increases, the full (2^t) model space grows quickly. Restricting or regularizing the sharing patterns can therefore be both a scientific choice and a computational necessity.
The documented sblr() interface exposes sharing-model inputs such as models and pimodels. These describe the permitted patterns and their prior probabilities. Exact argument support and behavior should be checked for the selected experimental algorithm before a production analysis.

title: Multi-Trait Models
text:
Genetic, Effect, and Residual Covariance
Covariance matrices are central to multi-trait inference.

Active-effect covariance
The active-effect covariance, (_b), describes how non-zero marker effects vary together across traits. A positive off-diagonal entry favors effects with the same direction; a negative entry favors opposite directions. This covariance is conditional on the marker being active for the corresponding traits.


Genetic covariance
The aggregate genetic value is
[ _{} = . ]
Its covariance across traits depends on both the fitted marker effects and LD. Genetic covariance therefore summarizes the combined architecture rather than only the conditional covariance of active effects.


Residual covariance
Residual vectors are commonly modeled as
[ _r (, _e), ]
where (_e) captures cross-trait association not explained by the fitted marker effects. Environmental effects, unmodeled genetic effects, measurement processes, and shared individuals can all contribute.
Effect, genetic, and residual covariance answer different questions and should not be interpreted interchangeably.

title: Multi-Trait Models
text:
Individual-Level and Summary-Statistics MTBLR
At the individual level, joint MT-BLR uses () and () directly. With complete data, it can calculate all required within-trait and cross-trait products from the observed individuals.
At the summary-statistics level, the same calculations must be represented by compatible cross-products:
[ ^{T}, ^{T}, ^{T}. ]
These correspond to:

marker-by-trait cross-products, often denoted Xy or wy;
marker cross-products or LD;
the trait cross-product matrix SSY;
trait-specific sample sizes and, where needed, pairwise sample-overlap information.

For one trait, (y^{T}y) is a scalar. For several traits, (^{T}) contains both trait-specific sums of squares and cross-trait products. The off-diagonal terms are necessary for estimating and updating residual covariance.
The summary statistics, LD, sample sizes, trait order, marker order, and scaling assumptions must all be compatible. See Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics for the cross-product representation and Technical Appendix: Multi-Trait Overlap for the role of SSY and sample overlap.

title: Multi-Trait Models
text:
Sample Overlap in Practice
Full sample overlap is the simplest setting: all traits are measured on the same individuals, and SSY can be computed directly from the phenotype matrix. Cross-trait residual covariance then has a direct interpretation on that shared sample.
With partial overlap, each trait pair may share a different number of individuals. A pairwise overlap matrix, often denoted (_{}), records those counts. Cross-trait phenotype products or covariances then require explicit assumptions about the shared samples and trait scaling.
The current CSR multi-trait implementation is closest to a shared-LD, equal-sample-size setting. It consumes cross-trait phenotype information but does not expose a general Nmat-aware workflow for arbitrary partial overlap. Analyses with partial or uncertain overlap should therefore be treated as a technical extension, not as a routine current workflow.

title: Multi-Trait Models
text:
Simulation and Model Development
Simulation is useful for checking whether a proposed MT-BLR model can recover known sharing and covariance structures.
mtsim() simulates multiple traits with shared and trait-specific causal markers, target heritabilities, and target genetic and residual correlations. A short schematic call is:
sim <- mtsim(
  W = W,
  nt = 3,
  n_shared = 30,
  n_specific = 10,
  h2 = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.3),
  rg = target_rg,
  re = target_re,
  seed = 1
)
Simulation output can be used to compare target and realized covariance, inspect true marker-effect patterns, and assess recovery under different priors or LD approximations.
mtsim_annotation() extends this development setting with overlapping annotations and annotation-informed marker architectures. summarize_annotation_signal() can summarize the simulated signal. The current polished annotation workflows primarily fit single-trait or parallel single-trait CSR models; annotation-aware joint MT-BLR remains a research direction. See Annotation-Informed Models.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Annotation-informed Bayesian linear regression uses external marker annotations to structure priors over marker inclusion, effect variance, or mixture-component membership. The likelihood still comes from phenotype summary statistics and LD. Annotations change how prior probability and scale are distributed across markers before and during posterior sampling.
In sblr, the polished annotation workflows build on the CSR ST-BLR data contract:
This note explains the implemented public wrappers and places them within the broader empirical-Bayes and multi-trait framework preserved in the archived annotation draft. Full marker-update derivations and implementation sketches belong in Technical annotation priors; full stick-breaking details belong in Technical SBayesRC-style annotations.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Why Annotations Inform Priors
Markers are not exchangeable with respect to existing biological knowledge. They may lie in coding regions, regulatory regions, QTL intervals, conserved sequence, tissue-specific chromatin states, or other externally defined sets. Annotation-informed models ask whether that information should alter a marker’s prior probability of being active or the expected scale of an active effect.
For marker (i) and trait (t), useful prior quantities include:
\[
\pi_{it} = P(d_{it}=1),
\qquad
v_{b,it} = \operatorname{Var}(b_{it}\mid d_{it}=1),
\]
and, for mixture models, component probabilities ({itc}=P(c{it}=c)). In proposed multi-trait extensions, annotations could additionally influence marker-specific sharing-model probabilities or effect covariance matrices.
Annotation information can enter at different stages:

fixed/external: marker-specific priors are supplied before fitting;
empirical Bayes: priors are estimated from an earlier genomic or annotation-level analysis, then treated as fixed;
direct learned: annotation coefficients are updated inside the genomic sampler;
grouped: markers share parameters within one mutually exclusive group;
mixture-based: annotations determine probabilities of null and active effect-size components.

These approaches answer different questions and propagate different amounts of uncertainty. None makes annotation membership causal by itself.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
section: Annotation Matrix, Overlap, Centering, and Marker Ordering
text:
Annotation Matrix, Overlap, Centering, and Marker Ordering
Let (A) be an (m K) annotation matrix:
\[
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
A_{11} & \cdots & A_{1K}\\
\vdots &        & \vdots\\
A_{m1} & \cdots & A_{mK}
\end{bmatrix},
\]
where rows are markers and columns are annotations. Binary entries can encode set membership, while continuous columns can encode scores or measurements. Annotations may overlap: a marker can belong to several biological categories simultaneously.
Overlap is scientifically useful but complicates interpretation. A direct sum over each annotation double-counts markers in multiple sets and is not a strict variance partition. Conditional annotation models instead use the whole row (A_i) to estimate the contribution of one annotation while accounting for the others. Strongly correlated annotation columns can still make individual coefficients weakly identified.
All public annotation wrappers prepare A with the package’s annotation matrix helper. It:

requires one row per model marker;
reorders named rows to marker names when all names are available;
rejects non-finite values;
can add an intercept column;
can standardize non-binary columns;
optionally centers and standardizes binary columns.

Row order remains a hard correctness condition:
row i of A
    = row i of stats$wy and stats$ww
    = row/column i of sparse LD
    = row i of fit$bm and fit$dm
The workflow makes this explicit:
marker_id <- Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
A <- sim$annot
rownames(A) <- marker_id
stopifnot(nrow(A) == length(marker_id),
          identical(rownames(A), marker_id))
Preparation of stats, sparse LD, and marker order is described in Sparse-LD and BED workflows.
Centering has a statistical role beyond numerical convenience. If (z_{it}=A_i_t), a centered predictor is
\[
z_{it}^{\mathrm{centered}}
=
A_i\eta_t-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m A_j\eta_t.
\]
Combining a centered annotation predictor with a global prior tends to redistribute prior mass across markers rather than allowing annotations to change the overall sparsity or variance scale without constraint.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Plain/Global Prior Baseline
The baseline BayesC-style sparse prior gives markers a common active probability and active-effect variance:
\[
d_{it}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_t),
\qquad
b_{it}\mid d_{it}=1\sim N(0,v_{b,t}),
\qquad
b_{it}\mid d_{it}=0=0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
b_{it}\sim(1-\pi_t)\delta_0+\pi_tN(0,v_{b,t}).
\]
This is the comparison model for annotation-aware priors. If annotations have no effect, fixed marker priors reduce to common values, learned annotation coefficients remain near zero, all group parameters become similar, and SBayesRC-style component probabilities do not vary meaningfully by annotation profile.
Annotation models should therefore be compared with a plain CSR fit using compatible markers, LD, priors, and MCMC settings. Differences should not be attributed to annotations when the underlying data preparation or global architecture changed at the same time.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Fixed Marker-Specific Priors
stblr_csr_prior_annot() fits CSR ST-BLR using fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities, fixed variance multipliers, or both. It supports two routes:

supply fixed_pi_marker and fixed_vb_multiplier directly; or
supply A with fixed coefficients beta_pi and beta_vb, from which the wrapper constructs marker-specific priors.

For fixed annotation coefficients, the implemented construction centers the annotation linear predictors:
\[
\ell^{\pi}_{it}
=
A_i\beta_{\pi,t}
-\frac{1}{m}\sum_j A_j\beta_{\pi,t},
\]
then computes
\[
\pi_{it}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left\{\operatorname{logit}(\pi_t)+\ell^\pi_{it}\right\},
\]
bounded to pi_min and pi_max. The variance multiplier is
\[
\lambda_{it}
=
\exp\left(
A_i\beta_{v,t}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_j A_j\beta_{v,t}
\right),
\]
bounded to vb_multiplier_min and vb_multiplier_max, with (v_{b,it}=v_{b,t}_{it}).
The direct route is illustrated by the annotation workflow:
fit_fixed <- stblr_csr_prior_annot(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  A = A,
  fixed_pi_marker = sim$pi_marker,
  fixed_vb_multiplier = sim$vb_multiplier,
  use_pi_marker = TRUE,
  use_vb_multiplier = TRUE
)
Fixed priors are appropriate when prior values come from external biological knowledge, an independent study, cross-fitted estimates, or a deliberately separate empirical-Bayes stage. They are also the simplest way to test whether the sampler responds sensibly to known marker-specific prior structure.
The key limitation is uncertainty: once supplied, these values are treated as fixed during the genomic fit. If they were estimated from the same data, the final posterior does not automatically propagate that first-stage uncertainty.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Direct Learned Annotation Effects
stblr_csr_learn_annot() learns annotation effects while fitting marker effects. For each trait, it maintains annotation coefficient vectors ({,t}) and ({v,t}). The implemented marker-specific prior is conceptually
\[
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{it})
=
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_t)
+\operatorname{center}_i(A_i\eta_{\pi,t}),
\]
and
\[
v_{b,it}
=
v_{b,t}
\exp\{\operatorname{center}_i(A_i\eta_{v,t})\}.
\]
In the second expression, the exponential term is a multiplier of the global effect variance. The implementation caps probabilities and multipliers:
\[
\pi_{it}\in[\pi_{\min},\pi_{\max}],
\qquad
\frac{v_{b,it}}{v_{b,t}}
\in[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}].
\]
The sampler alternates between marker updates under current marker-specific priors and annotation-coefficient updates. At intervals controlled by annot_update_every, random-walk proposals perturb ({,t}) or ({v,t}). The inclusion-coefficient target uses current inclusion states, while the variance-coefficient target uses current active effects. Gaussian shrinkage scales sigma_eta_pi and sigma_eta_vb regularize the coefficients; proposal scales rw_sd_eta_pi and rw_sd_eta_vb control Metropolis movement.
fit_learned <- stblr_csr_learn_annot(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  A = A,
  learn_pi_annot = TRUE,
  learn_vb_annot = TRUE,
  rw_sd_eta_pi = 0.02,
  rw_sd_eta_vb = 0.02,
  annot_update_every = 10
)
The fit reports posterior annotation coefficients as eta_pi and eta_vb. They should be interpreted jointly with annotation scaling, coefficient shrinkage, bounds, proposal behavior, marker-level posterior summaries, and convergence diagnostics.
Use the learned model when annotation effects are genuinely part of the inferential target and there is enough information to estimate them. It is more coherent than treating same-data estimates as fixed, but also more demanding: overlapping annotations, weak signals, poor proposal scales, and short chains can produce unstable or poorly mixed coefficient estimates.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Group Priors
stblr_csr_group_annot() assigns every marker to exactly one group and gives each group trait-specific prior parameters. If (g(i)) is marker (i)’s group index, the prior is
\[
d_{it}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{g(i),t}),
\qquad
b_{it}\mid d_{it}=1
\sim N\left(0,v_{b,t}\lambda_{g(i),t}\right).
\]
The R wrapper accepts a length-(m) group vector, optionally named by marker. It converts group labels into an internal zero-based group_index, records group names and sizes, initializes group_pi and group_vb_multiplier, and returns group-level posterior summaries including included-marker counts.
group <- ifelse(A[, "Anno1"] != 0, "annotated", "background")
names(group) <- rownames(A)

fit_group <- stblr_csr_group_annot(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  group = group,
  group_pi_init = c(0.002, 0.001),
  group_vb_multiplier_init = c(1.1, 1.0),
  updatePi = TRUE,
  updateGroupVb = TRUE
)
Group inclusion probabilities have group-specific beta-prior controls. Variance multipliers can be updated and optionally normalized. Small groups need especially strong regularization because their inclusion counts and variance estimates are noisy.
Group priors are useful when categories are naturally mutually exclusive or when a simple, auditable model is preferred. They are also a practical simplification of overlapping annotations: define a deterministic hierarchy or a small set of combined categories, then fit one group per marker. That simplification discards overlap structure and makes results depend on the assignment rule. When overlap itself is scientifically important, learned matrix-based or SBayesRC-style models are usually more appropriate.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
SBayesRC-Style Overlapping-Annotation Mixture Priors
stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic() replaces a single active-effect distribution with multiple variance components. Let
\[
\gamma=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_C),
\qquad
\gamma_1=0,\quad \gamma_c>0\text{ for }c>1,
\]
where the zero component is null and active components scale the marker-effect variance. A common workflow choice is gamma = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1).
This is an SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior. Its core prior family is closely aligned with the published SBayesRC prior structure: marker effects follow a BayesR-like mixture, and marker-specific component probabilities use conditional probit stick-breaking regressions on annotations. It is not an exact reproduction of GCTB SBayesRC as exposed by default. The public wrapper uses the four-component gamma grid above, whereas published SBayesRC uses c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1). In addition, sblr uses a CSR sparse-LD likelihood rather than GCTB’s low-rank rotated summary-statistics likelihood. Users can explicitly request the published gamma grid:
fit_sbayesrc_published_gamma <- stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  A = A,
  gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
)
Matching the gamma grid aligns that part of the prior specification; it does not make the complete implementation identical to GCTB SBayesRC.
For marker (i), annotations determine component probabilities through a generalized probit stick-breaking construction. Let
\[
\eta_i=A_i\alpha,
\qquad
p_{ij}=\Phi(\eta_{ij}),
\]
for (C-1) stick-breaking steps. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i1} &= 1-p_{i1},\\
\pi_{i2} &= p_{i1}(1-p_{i2}),\\
&\ \vdots\\
\pi_{iC} &= \prod_{j=1}^{C-1}p_{ij}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The probabilities are non-negative and sum to one. The native sampler floors and renormalizes them for numerical stability. Marker (i)’s expected gamma multiplier is
\[
E(\gamma_i\mid A_i,\alpha)
=
\sum_{c=1}^C\pi_{ic}\gamma_c.
\]
make_sbayesrc_alpha_init() creates deterministic initial values. It distributes the initial active probability across non-null components, converts those marginal probabilities into conditional stick-breaking probabilities, and, when an all-ones intercept exists, encodes the baseline in that intercept row of alpha_init. Other coefficients begin at zero unless supplied.
fit_sbayesrc <- stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  A = A,
  gamma = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1),
  updateAlpha = TRUE,
  alpha_update_every = 10
)
The fit contains annotation coefficients alpha, annotation-effect variances sigmaSqAlpha, marker component probabilities comp_prob, and component counts ncomp.
The exported diagnostic helpers convert fitted coefficients into compact, deterministic summaries:

sbayesrc_annotation_pi(alpha, gamma) applies stick-breaking to each annotation coefficient row;
sbayesrc_annotation_gamma_mean(alpha, gamma) returns expected gamma per annotation row;
sbayesrc_marker_pi(A, alpha, gamma) applies stick-breaking to (A), returning marker-level component probabilities;
sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(A, alpha, gamma) returns expected gamma per marker.

Annotation-row diagnostics isolate one coefficient row and are not the same as marker-level predictions under overlapping annotation profiles. For biological interpretation, inspect both, and compare marker expected gamma with posterior inclusion probabilities without assuming they should be identical.
Use the SBayesRC-style model when annotations may overlap and the scientific question concerns how annotations shift probability among null, small, moderate, and larger effect components. It is more expressive than a binary active/null model and correspondingly needs careful prior, mixing, and identifiability diagnostics.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Annotation Workflow
The current workflow connects simulation, CSR preparation, four models, and compact diagnostics:
mtsim_annotation()
    -> summarize_annotation_signal()
    -> bed_xtx_xty() + sparseLD_stream_CSR()
    -> align A with stats and sparse LD
    -> stblr_csr_prior_annot()
    -> stblr_csr_learn_annot()
    -> stblr_csr_group_annot()
    -> stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic()
    -> compact fit, annotation, and expected-gamma summaries
mtsim_annotation() simulates phenotypes, marker effects, overlapping annotations, enriched causal-marker sampling, and marker-specific prior values. It supports known-truth checks but does not represent a real-data validation by itself.
summarize_annotation_signal(sim) reports annotation sizes, causal counts, and causal rates. With a fit, it can add trait-specific mean posterior inclusion and mean absolute posterior effect summaries. These summaries are descriptive: annotation overlap and LD mean they are not additive variance partitions.
The workflow then constructs stats and ld_prefix from the same BED marker order, verifies A, and fits all four prior families. Full marker matrices remain available in fit objects, while compact summaries prevent marker-scale output from flooding the console. See Workflows and outputs for reporting patterns.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Empirical-Bayes Annotation Workflows
The archived annotation draft describes a broader staged strategy:
\[
\text{genomic STBLR/MTBLR}
\rightarrow
\text{marker-level posterior summaries}
\rightarrow
\text{annotation-level model}
\rightarrow
\text{annotation-informed priors}
\rightarrow
\text{next genomic fit}.
\]
First-stage summaries can include posterior means (b_{it}), posterior inclusion probabilities (_{it}), residual scores, and set-specific genomic variance contributions. For an annotation set (S_k), a smoothed inclusion estimate is
\[
\widehat\pi_{k,t}
=
\frac{\alpha+\sum_{i\in S_k}\widehat{dm}_{it}}
{2\alpha+|S_k|}.
\]
An effect-scale estimate can use the estimated set contribution
\[
\widehat V_{G,k,t}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in S_k}
\widehat b_{it}(wy_{it}-r_{it})
\]
and divide by an effective number of active markers,
\[
m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}
=
\sum_{i\in S_k}\widehat{dm}_{it},
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2_{b,k,t}
=
\frac{\widehat V_{G,k,t}}
{\max(m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t},c)}.
\]
For overlapping annotations, marker-level responses such as ({it}), (b{it}^2), or estimated variance contributions can be regressed jointly on (A). The resulting coefficients can construct marker-specific priors on logit or log scales.
This strategy preserves useful technical ideas for prior learning, annotation-level STBLR/MTBLR, multi-trait sharing priors, and warm starts. However, it is not identical to the four implemented direct workflow wrappers. When the same data estimate priors and evaluate the final model, uncertainty can be understated. Sample splitting, chromosome-wise cross-fitting, external estimates, or a fully hierarchical model are more conservative alternatives.

title: Annotation-Informed Models
text:
Choosing an Annotation Model









Model
Use when
Main advantage
Main caution




Fixed marker-specific prior
Reliable external, cross-fitted, or deliberately staged priors already exist; or a known-prior simulation is being checked.
Stable and auditable; simplest marker-specific model.
Treats prior values as known and does not propagate their estimation uncertainty.


Learned annotation coefficients
Inclusion or effect-scale annotation effects are inferential targets and sufficient signal exists to estimate them.
Learns annotation effects jointly with marker effects.
Requires careful shrinkage, proposal tuning, bounds, and convergence assessment.


Group prior
Markers belong to one meaningful category each, or a simple mutually exclusive approximation is acceptable.
Easy to interpret and computationally direct.
Discards or arbitrarily resolves overlapping annotations; small groups are unstable.


SBayesRC-style mixture prior
Overlapping annotations should shift probability among null and multiple active-effect scales.
Flexible effect-size architecture with marker-level mixture probabilities.
More parameters and more difficult identifiability and mixing diagnostics.


Empirical-Bayes staged prior
First-stage genomic evidence should inform later fits or proposed MTBLR extensions.
Flexible bridge between posterior summaries and future priors.
Same-data reuse can be optimistic; many draft components remain research-stage.



Start with the simplest model that matches the scientific question. More expressive annotation models do not automatically produce more reliable biological conclusions.

title: Data Representations
text:
sblr can fit Bayesian linear regression models from two broad forms of genomic data:
These are two representations of closely related regression calculations, not two unrelated model families. The representation determines what must be stored, what can be recomputed during sampling, and which alignment and sample-overlap assumptions must be made explicit.

title: Data Representations
text:
Individual-Level PLINK BED Representation
Let (X) be an (n m) genotype matrix for (n) individuals and (m) markers, and let (Y) be an (n n_t) phenotype matrix for (n_t) traits. For one trait, (Y) reduces to a vector (y). A Bayesian linear regression model can be written as
\[
Y = XB + E,
\]
where (B) contains marker effects and (E) contains residuals. In a single-trait model, this is (y = Xb + e).
With individual-level data, a marker update can read the observed genotype column (x_j) and evaluate quantities such as
\[
x_j^\top x_j
\quad\text{and}\quad
x_j^\top e
=
x_j^\top(y-Xb).
\]
The sampler can therefore update effects from observed marker values and current individual-level residuals. It does not need a separately supplied LD matrix because correlations among markers are implicit in (X).
PLINK BED files store genotype calls compactly on disk rather than as an in-memory numeric matrix. In the package workflow, a qgg Glist supplies the BED file paths and related metadata:

Glist$bedfiles identifies the BED files;
Glist$n gives the number of individuals;
Glist$rsids identifies the marker columns in each BED file;
Glist$af supplies allele frequencies used when markers are standardized;
Glist$rsidsLD identifies the selected markers and their intended LD order.

stblr_bed_marker() fits directly from this representation. It receives the Glist, phenotype vector or matrix y, chromosome selection, and marker column indices cls. Its BED samplers read marker blocks from disk and perform marker updates without first materializing all of (X) or a full (X^X) matrix. Optional rows select 1-based individual indices, and scale = TRUE standardizes markers using the corresponding allele frequencies.
The individual-level representation is information-rich: if the same individuals have multiple measured traits, cross-trait phenotype and residual cross-products can be calculated directly. Its main costs are access to sensitive individual-level data and repeated genotype reading during model fitting.

title: Data Representations
text:
Dense Summary-Statistic Representation
The Gaussian linear model likelihood and marker-update calculations can be expressed using cross-products. For one trait, the central quantities are
\[
wy = X^\top y,
\qquad
XX = X^\top X,
\qquad
yy = y^\top y,
\]
together with the sample size (n). For multiple traits,
\[
WY = X^\top Y
\]
contains one marker-trait cross-product column per trait.
The matrix (X^X) describes both marker sums of squares on its diagonal and marker-marker LD in its off-diagonal entries. In package interfaces, ww denotes per-trait marker sums of squares or corresponding diagonal information, while LD supplies the off-diagonal relationships needed to propagate an effect update to correlated markers. Depending on scaling and the producing function, LD may be represented in correlation units or as the corresponding genotype cross-products. The statistics and LD representation must use the same marker scaling and order.
These quantities are sufficient for many marker updates because the current marker-residual score can be represented as
\[
r = X^\top(y-Xb) = wy - X^\top Xb.
\]
If marker (j)’s effect changes by (b_j), the updated score can be calculated from column (j) of (X^X):
\[
r_{\text{new}}
=
r_{\text{old}} - (X^\top X)_{\cdot j}\Delta b_j.
\]
This is why a summary-statistics sampler needs more than marginal genotype-phenotype associations. It needs enough information to reproduce the cross-products used by the marker-update and variance calculations. Marginal wy values without compatible LD cannot account for correlated markers, and LD without wy, yy, and (n) does not define the phenotype side of the likelihood.
A dense representation stores all of (X^X), which requires (O(m^2)) entries. That becomes impractical for large marker sets. The disk-backed sparse-LD representation retains the same conceptual role while dropping small or distant marker-marker entries.

title: Data Representations
text:
Disk-Backed CSR Sparse-LD Representation
Compressed sparse row (CSR) format stores only retained entries of a sparse matrix. Conceptually, it records:

a vector of row pointers delimiting each matrix row;
column indices for retained entries; and
the retained LD or cross-product values.

sparseLD_stream_CSR() computes sparse LD directly from one or more PLINK BED files and writes a disk-backed CSR representation at out_prefix. The selected marker columns are supplied as a list through cls, one vector per BED file. Optional rows and af must describe the same individuals and marker scaling used for the sufficient statistics.
Sparsification is controlled by:

r2_threshold, which removes pairs below a squared-correlation threshold;
max_distance_bp, which can restrict pairs by base-pair distance;
max_distance_variants, which can restrict pairs by marker-index distance;
block_size and nthreads, which control construction rather than the statistical definition.

The sparse representation approximates (X^X). It reduces memory and disk requirements when most long-range or weak marker relationships can be ignored, but the threshold and distance rules become part of the analysis. Two fits using different sparse-LD construction rules do not have identical inputs even if they began from the same BED file.
sparseLD_read_CSR() reads files written by sparseLD_stream_CSR() and returns row pointers, column indices, and values. Its one_based option controls the indexing convention of returned column indices. This reader is useful for checking dimensions, indexing, and retained entries; stblr_csr() uses the disk-backed prefix directly.
Detailed storage and construction contracts belong in Technical sparse LD and CSR.

title: Data Representations
section: Sufficient Statistics: wy, ww, and yy
text:
Sufficient Statistics: wy, ww, and yy
bed_xtx_xty() is the package bridge from individual-level BED data and phenotypes to the sufficient statistics consumed by stblr_csr(). It accepts a BED file, the total number of individuals, selected BED marker columns cls, corresponding allele frequencies af, and a phenotype matrix y. Optional rows and scale determine which individuals and marker standardization are used.
The returned stats object contains the marker-trait cross-products and related quantities required by the ST-BLR wrapper:

stats$wy: (X^Y), represented by trait;
stats$ww: marker sums of squares or diagonal genotype cross-product information, represented by trait;
stats$yy: (y_t^y_t) for each trait;
stats$n and stats$m, when available, for sample and marker counts.

stblr_csr() combines this object with ld_prefix, the prefix written by sparseLD_stream_CSR(). The wrapper initializes per-trait variance quantities using stats$yy, (n), and (m), then passes wy, ww, yy, and the CSR prefix to the sparse-LD sampler.
The complete conceptual bridge is:
BED files + aligned phenotypes
          |
          +--> bed_xtx_xty() --------> wy, ww, yy, n
          |
          +--> sparseLD_stream_CSR() -> disk-backed sparse X'X / LD
                                         |
                                         v
                         stblr_csr() summary-statistics model
The two branches must be produced from the same marker selection, sample selection, allele frequencies, and scaling convention. In contrast, stblr_bed_marker() follows a direct branch from BED files and phenotypes to the individual-level sampler. The worked comparison is described in Sparse-LD and BED workflows.

title: Data Representations
section: Multi-Trait Cross-Products, Sample Overlap, and SSY
text:
Multi-Trait Cross-Products, Sample Overlap, and SSY
The phrase “multi-trait summary statistics” can refer to two different levels of information.
First, traits can be fitted as separate or parallel single-trait regressions. For trait (t), the phenotype sum of squares is
\[
yy_t = y_t^\top y_t = \sum_i y_{it}^2.
\]
A vector of yy values, with corresponding columns of (X^Y), is enough to initialize and fit per-trait likelihood calculations that do not require observed cross-trait phenotype products. The current stblr_csr() wrapper uses this per-trait representation: it infers the number of traits from length(stats$yy) and uses each yy_t to initialize trait-specific variances.
Second, a genuinely joint multi-trait likelihood with a full residual covariance matrix requires the cross-trait phenotype matrix
\[
\mathrm{SSY} = Y^\top Y,
\qquad
\mathrm{SSY}_{ts}
=
\sum_{i \in \mathcal I_{ts}} y_{it}y_{is},
\]
where (I_{ts}) is the set of individuals observed for both traits. The diagonal entries are the univariate yy_t; the off-diagonal entries contain information that a vector of yy values does not preserve.
With individual-level (Y), SSY and the effective overlap counts can be calculated from observed individuals. With summary statistics, they must be provided or reconstructed. If (N_{ts}) is the number of individuals shared by traits (t) and (s), and (R_y) is a phenotypic correlation matrix, a common approximation is
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{SSY}}
=
N \odot \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(Y),
\]
with diagonals forced to the observed yy_t. This approximation assumes that overlap counts and phenotypic covariance information are meaningful for the study design. Full overlap, partial overlap, missingness, and meta-analysis can imply materially different (N) matrices.
Without cross-trait SSY and overlap information, a summary-statistics model cannot reconstruct the cross-products needed for full residual covariance updates. The complete derivation and assumptions are preserved in Technical multi-trait sample overlap.

title: Data Representations
text:
Marker Ordering and Annotation Alignment
Marker order is a correctness condition, not presentation metadata. Every marker-indexed object must refer to the same biological marker at position (j):
BED marker column selected by cls
    = Glist$rsidsLD marker j
    = sufficient-statistic row j
    = sparse-LD row and column j
    = annotation-matrix row j
    = posterior-summary row j
In the workflows, the intended LD marker order is established by Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]. The BED column indices are derived with
cls <- match(Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]], Glist$rsids[[chr]])
stopifnot(!anyNA(cls))
The same cls is then supplied to bed_xtx_xty() and, as a list, sparseLD_stream_CSR(). Allele frequencies are subset with the same indices. For annotation models, the (m K) annotation matrix A must have one row per selected marker in exactly this order. The annotation workflow makes that contract explicit by assigning Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]] as row names and checking that they are identical to the expected marker IDs.
Posterior matrices such as fit$bm and fit$dm inherit the marker ordering used by the model input. A plausible-looking result is still invalid if its rows are joined to annotations or marker metadata in a different order.
Sample alignment is equally important. When rows is used, the phenotype rows and every BED-derived object must describe the same individuals. Sufficient statistics generated from one sample subset cannot be combined with sparse LD generated from another without changing the implied model.

title: Model Overview
text:
sblr is an experimental R package for Bayesian linear regression of genomic marker effects. Its models estimate marker effects, posterior inclusion probabilities, and variance or covariance components from either individual-level PLINK BED data or summary statistics combined with linkage disequilibrium (LD).
The package landscape is easiest to understand along three axes:
These axes describe different choices. For example, a model can be single-trait, use summary statistics with disk-backed sparse LD, and use an annotation-informed prior. This note maps those choices to the current public functions and to the notes that explain them in detail.

title: Model Overview
text:
Common Model: (y = Xb + e)
For one trait, the common regression model is
\[
y = Xb + e,
\]
where (X) is an (n m) genotype matrix, (b) is a vector of marker effects, and (e) is residual variation. Bayesian genomic regression combines this likelihood with a prior on marker effects and, often, latent inclusion indicators.
For (n_t) traits, the model becomes
\[
Y = XB + E,
\]
where each row of (B) is a marker-effect vector across traits. A genuinely joint multi-trait model can describe covariance among effects, residuals, or trait-sharing patterns. Running one single-trait model per phenotype can be useful and parallelizable, but it is not equivalent to a joint multi-trait likelihood.
The main posterior marker summaries are:
\[
\widehat b_{it} = E(b_{it}\mid\text{data})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\widehat{dm}_{it} = P(d_{it}=1\mid\text{data}),
\]
represented in fitted objects by bm and dm. Depending on the wrapper, fits also contain sampled effects and indicators, variance traces, covariance summaries, prior parameters, and model-specific annotation diagnostics.

title: Model Overview
section: Three Axes for Choosing a Model
text:
Three Axes for Choosing a Model

Single-Trait Versus Multi-Trait
Single-trait BLR/ST-BLR estimates scalar effects and inclusion probabilities for one phenotype. Current BED, CSR, and annotation workflow examples are centered on this model family. Several ST-BLR wrappers accept a phenotype matrix or multiple trait-specific sufficient-statistic columns, but their marker-update structure should not automatically be interpreted as a full joint MTBLR sharing model.
Multi-trait BLR (MTBLR) treats marker effects as vectors and can model effect covariance, residual covariance, and explicit trait-sharing models. The public sblr() interface accepts summary-statistics inputs such as a trait cross-product matrix yy, marker-trait cross-products Xy, LD or marker cross-products XX, and optional multi-trait inclusion models. Full summary-statistics residual-covariance modeling additionally depends on cross-trait phenotype products and sample-overlap assumptions.
The current most polished end-to-end workflows are BED/CSR ST-BLR and annotation-informed CSR ST-BLR. Multi-trait theory remains central to the package and motivates the covariance outputs, simulation tools, and proposed annotation-aware extensions. Read Multi-trait models before interpreting trait sharing or covariance as a joint model result.


Individual-Level Versus Summary Statistics
With individual-level data, the sampler can read observed genotype columns from BED files and calculate marker-update quantities directly. The principal public interface is stblr_bed_marker().
With summary statistics, the sampler instead receives cross-products:
\[
wy = X^\top y,
\qquad
ww_j = x_j^\top x_j,
\qquad
yy = y^\top y,
\]
plus compatible LD and sample size (n). The residual score can be maintained as
\[
r = X^\top y - X^\top Xb.
\]
stblr_csr() uses sufficient statistics from bed_xtx_xty() with a disk-backed sparse-LD prefix written by sparseLD_stream_CSR(). The public sblr() interface represents the broader summary-statistics model family and accepts dense or sparse marker cross-product structures through XX.
These representations, their information requirements, and sample-overlap issues are covered in Data representations. The practical BED-to-CSR handoff is covered in Sparse-LD and BED workflows.


Plain Versus Annotation-Informed Priors
A plain/global prior gives markers a common prior architecture, such as a global inclusion probability and marker-effect variance. A BayesC-style spike-and-slab representation is
\[
d_{it} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_t),
\qquad
b_{it}\mid d_{it}=1 \sim N(0,v_{b,t}),
\qquad
b_{it}\mid d_{it}=0 = 0.
\]
An annotation-informed prior allows prior inclusion probabilities, variance scales, or mixture-component probabilities to vary by marker, marker group, or annotation profile. Current public CSR wrappers distinguish four implemented forms:

fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities or variance multipliers;
group-level priors;
directly learned annotation effects on inclusion or variance;
SBayesRC-style mixture probabilities learned from overlapping annotations.

These models use annotation information as a prior or evidence structure. They do not by themselves establish that an annotation is causal. The empirical-Bayes and proposed multi-trait annotation extensions in the source drafts remain important technical directions, but they should be distinguished from currently implemented public wrappers.

Practical Workflow Families
The package’s current workflows can be read as five connected families.

Direct BED Individual-Level ST-BLR
Use stblr_bed_marker() when BED genotypes and aligned phenotypes remain available during fitting. Genotypes are read in blocks, and a separate LD artifact is not required.


BED to Sufficient Statistics and Sparse LD
Use bed_xtx_xty() to derive wy, ww, and yy from BED data and phenotypes. Use sparseLD_stream_CSR() to derive disk-backed sparse LD from the same markers, samples, allele frequencies, and scaling convention. This preparation workflow creates reusable inputs for CSR models.


CSR Summary-Statistics ST-BLR
Use stblr_csr() with the sufficient-statistics object and sparse-LD prefix. This path is appropriate when the prepared cross-products and LD files should be reused without repeated BED access during fitting.


Annotation-Informed CSR ST-BLR
Start from the same stats and ld_prefix, then add marker-aligned annotation information or marker-specific priors. Choose among fixed, learned, group, and SBayesRC-style wrappers according to the intended prior architecture.


Simulation and Model Checking
Use mtsim() to simulate multi-trait phenotypes, marker effects, and known shared or trait-specific signals. Use mtsim_annotation() to additionally simulate overlapping annotations, causal enrichment, and marker-specific prior values. Simulation outputs provide known truth for checking marker recovery, annotation summaries, model behavior, and BED-versus-CSR preparation.
Simulation is a model-checking tool, not evidence that the same assumptions hold in real data.

title: Model Overview
Model Overview
text:
What Is Not Guaranteed

BED and CSR fits are not exactly equal. Under matched markers, rows, scaling, priors, and MCMC settings they should agree qualitatively, but sparse-LD approximation, update scheduling, floating-point precision, and Monte Carlo variation prevent exact equality.
CSR disk internals are not a manual file-format API. Use package writers, readers, and model wrappers rather than editing row-pointer, column-index, value, or metadata files directly.
Annotation effects are not causal proof. Enrichment, learned prior coefficients, posterior inclusion, and shared genetic signals can generate hypotheses but do not identify causal biological mechanisms by themselves.
Short workflow chains are not final inference. Demonstration settings establish object handoffs and model execution. Real analyses require longer chains, convergence assessment, sensitivity analysis, and posterior predictive checks.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
The single-trait Bayesian linear regression (ST-BLR) layer is the common statistical foundation for the direct BED, summary-statistics CSR, scheduled sparse-update, and annotation-informed workflows in sblr. These interfaces use different data representations and prior refinements, but they share the same basic objective: estimate sparse marker effects for one phenotype while accounting for linkage disequilibrium (LD).
This note defines that core model, explains the quantities used by marker updates, and distinguishes statistical prior choices from computational scheduling controls. Data preparation and complete workflows are covered in Data representations and Sparse-LD and BED workflows.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Single-Trait Regression Model
For (n) individuals and (m) markers, let (y) be an (n)-vector of phenotypes and (X) an (n m) genotype matrix. The single-trait linear model is
\[
y = Xb + e,
\]
where

(b=(b_1,,b_m)^) contains marker effects;
(eN(0,v_e I_n)) is residual variation;
(v_e) is the residual variance; and
the genetic value (g=Xb) has variance (v_g).

When genotypes and phenotypes are centered, a realized genetic-variance quantity can be written as
\[
v_g(b)
=
\frac{1}{n}b^\top X^\top Xb.
\]
This is distinct from the active marker-effect prior variance (v_b). Informally, (v_b) controls the scale of nonzero effects before seeing the data, while (v_g) describes the aggregate variation generated by all marker effects and LD.
Although several ST-BLR wrappers accept multiple phenotype columns, their basic marker updates remain trait-specific. Running these updates for several traits is not automatically equivalent to a joint multi-trait model with effect or residual covariance. See Multi-trait models for that distinction.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Summary-Statistics Representation
The Gaussian regression calculations can be expressed using cross-products:
\[
wy = X^\top y,
\qquad
XX = X^\top X,
\qquad
yy = y^\top y.
\]
Let
\[
w_i = x_i^\top x_i
\]
be marker (i)’s diagonal genotype cross-product. The marker-scale residual score vector is
\[
r = X^\top(y-Xb)=wy-XXb.
\]
For marker (i), the partial residual score that adds its current effect back is
\[
s_i = r_i + w_i b_i.
\]
These quantities contain the information needed for a single-marker update: wy connects markers to the phenotype, (XX) propagates effect changes through LD, (w_i) controls the conditional precision, and yy contributes to residual-variance calculations and initialization. If (b_i) changes by (b_i), the residual score can be updated without revisiting individual-level observations:
\[
r_{\mathrm{new}}
=
r_{\mathrm{old}}-XX_{\cdot i}\Delta b_i.
\]
stblr_csr() uses stats$wy, stats$ww, stats$yy, sample size (n), and a disk-backed sparse approximation to (XX). The complete sufficient- statistic and sparse-storage contracts are described in Technical summary statistics and Technical sparse LD and CSR.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Global BayesC-Style Sparse Prior
The baseline ST-BLR prior represents every marker as either null or active. Introduce an inclusion indicator
\[
d_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi),
\]
and write
\[
b_i=d_i\alpha_i,
\qquad
\alpha_i\mid d_i=1\sim N(0,v_b).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
b_i\sim(1-\pi)\delta_0+\pi N(0,v_b),
\]
where (_0) is a point mass at zero. The global parameters have different roles:

() is the prior probability that a marker is active;
(v_b) is the prior variance of an active marker effect;
(v_e) is the residual variance;
(v_g) is the genetic variance generated by the fitted marker effects.

The wrapper argument pi_marker is a backward-compatible initial active probability. Current wrappers separate related roles through pi_init, pi_vb_init, pi_prior_mean, and beta-prior controls. In particular, the initial active-effect variance is scaled from the initial heritability and expected number of active markers:
\[
v_b^{(0)}
\approx
\frac{v_y h^2}{m\pi_{\mathrm{vb}}},
\]
where (v_y) is the phenotype variance and ({}) corresponds to pi_vb_init. This is an initialization and prior-scale choice, not a statement that exactly (m{}) markers are causal.

Marker Inclusion Update
Under the global prior, the marginal log Bayes factor for marker (i) can be written as
\[
\log BF_i
=
\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{v_e}{v_e+w_i v_b}\right)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{s_i^2v_b}{v_e(v_e+w_i v_b)}.
\]
Combining this evidence with the prior odds gives
\[
P(d_i=1\mid -)
=
\frac{\pi BF_i}{(1-\pi)+\pi BF_i}.
\]
Conditional on inclusion, the marker effect has Gaussian full conditional
\[
b_i\mid d_i=1,-
\sim
N\left(
\frac{s_i}{w_i+v_e/v_b},
\frac{v_e}{w_i+v_e/v_b}
\right).
\]
If excluded, (b_i=0). Repeated MCMC updates produce the posterior inclusion probability (PIP)
\[
\operatorname{PIP}_i
=
P(d_i=1\mid y,X,\text{prior}),
\]
and posterior mean effect
\[
\widehat b_i=E(b_i\mid y,X,\text{prior}).
\]
In fit objects these are generally returned as rows of dm and bm. PIPs quantify posterior evidence under the chosen data representation, LD, prior, and sampler. They are not probabilities that a marker is biologically causal.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Two Fitted Representations

Individual-Level BED: stblr_bed_marker()
stblr_bed_marker() fits ST-BLR directly from PLINK BED markers referenced by a qgg Glist. It reads selected genotype columns during sampling and maintains individual-level residual information. A short illustrative call is:
fit_bed <- stblr_bed_marker(
  Glist = Glist,
  y = y,
  chr = 1,
  cls = cls,
  pi_marker = 0.001,
  h2 = 0.5,
  scheduled = TRUE,
  nit = 1000,
  nburn = 100
)
This path is appropriate when individual-level genotypes remain available and repeated BED access is acceptable. The statistical inputs include the phenotype, selected samples and markers, allele frequencies, and genotype scaling choice. A separately materialized LD matrix is not required because LD is present in the observed genotype columns.


Summary Statistics and CSR LD: stblr_csr()
stblr_csr() fits the same broad global-prior ST-BLR family using BED-derived or otherwise compatible sufficient statistics and disk-backed sparse LD:
fit_csr <- stblr_csr(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  n = n,
  pi_marker = 0.001,
  h2 = 0.5,
  scheduled = FALSE,
  nit = 1000,
  nburn = 100
)
Here stats$wy, stats$ww, and stats$yy replace repeated phenotype and diagonal genotype calculations, while ld_prefix supplies retained off-diagonal LD relationships. The CSR representation makes large sparse-LD analyses possible without loading dense (XX) into memory.
The two paths target closely related single-trait sparse-regression models when samples, markers, scaling, priors, and likelihood information are matched. They are not expected to produce identical Monte Carlo output. Thresholded sparse LD approximates the full genotype cross-products, and the implementations can differ in residual maintenance, update order, scheduling, floating-point behavior, and initialization. Finite MCMC variation adds further differences.
Use BED-versus-CSR agreement as an integration and sensitivity diagnostic. Compare broad posterior patterns, PIP rankings, effects, and variance summaries rather than expecting equality of individual draws.

title: Single-Trait Models
section: Scheduled Sparse Updates and Runtime Controls
text:
Scheduled Sparse Updates and Runtime Controls
Most markers in a sparse model spend substantial time in the null state. Updating every null marker on every iteration can dominate runtime. Scheduled samplers reduce this work by revisiting low-priority null markers less often while retaining mechanisms that periodically reconsider them.
These settings are computational controls, not definitions of a different prior. They do not replace the BayesC-style (), (v_b), or (v_e) parameters. They do, however, change the update schedule and can affect finite-run behavior, mixing, and approximation quality. Aggressive skipping therefore requires convergence and sensitivity checks.

Common Scheduling Controls







Control
High-level role




scheduled
Selects the scheduled sampler path where supported.


full_sweep_every
Forces periodic reconsideration of all markers rather than only scheduled or active candidates.


null_skip_base
Sets a baseline interval for revisiting low-probability null markers in scheduled samplers.


null_skip_max
Caps adaptive null-marker skip intervals.


candidate_threshold
Treats markers with sufficiently large current inclusion probability as candidates for more frequent updates.


candidate_lifetime
Keeps candidates active for a number of scheduled sweeps after they were last considered interesting.


skip_nulls_burnin_only
Restricts null-marker skipping to burn-in when TRUE, so retained sampling uses the less aggressive post-burn-in schedule.



The BED non-scheduled sparse path also exposes null_update_prob, which controls probabilistic revisiting of null markers. BED samplers use rebuild_every to periodically rebuild individual-level residual state.


CSR LD-Neighbor Wake-Up
The scheduled CSR sampler additionally exposes:

wakeup_ld_neighbors, which allows a marker update to reschedule retained LD neighbors;
wakeup_diff_threshold, which requires a sufficiently large effect change before triggering neighbor wake-up; and
wakeup_max_neighbors, which can cap the number of neighbors rescheduled.

The motivation is that changing one marker’s effect changes the residual scores of correlated markers. Waking LD neighbors lets the schedule respond to that local change without immediately performing a complete sweep.
For validation, compare scheduled and unscheduled runs under matched priors and data, inspect sensitivity to full-sweep frequency and skip settings, and use sufficiently long retained sampling. Runtime improvement alone does not establish that posterior exploration is adequate.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Variance Updates and Interpretation
The public wrappers initialize marker-effect and residual variance structures from phenotype variance, h2, marker count, and inclusion-prior controls. During sampling, updateB, updateE, and updatePi determine whether the corresponding quantities are updated. The degrees-of-freedom controls nub and nue and associated scale matrices define their priors.
For one trait, covariance matrices reduce conceptually to scalar variance quantities, although formatted fits may retain matrix-shaped summaries for consistency with multi-trait code. Distinguish:

the active marker-effect variance (v_b);
aggregate genetic variance (v_g);
residual variance (v_e); and
their MCMC traces and posterior summaries.

Initial h2 helps set starting and prior scales. It is not guaranteed to equal the posterior or realized heritability. In simulations, differences can arise from finite data, realized architecture, shrinkage, sparse LD, and Monte Carlo variation.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Posterior Outputs and Diagnostics
Formatted ST-BLR fits are named lists. Components depend on the wrapper and sampler path, so inspect names(fit) and fit$input before interpreting them.







Component
Single-trait interpretation




bm
Posterior mean marker effects.


dm
Posterior inclusion probabilities or retained inclusion summaries.


b
Current or returned marker-effect state, when returned.


d
Current or returned inclusion state, when returned.


r
Marker-scale residual score state, when returned.


vbs
Retained trace of active marker-effect variance.


vgs
Retained trace of genetic variance.


ves
Retained trace of residual variance.


pi
Final or current inclusion-probability summary, when returned.


pim
Posterior mean inclusion-probability summary, when returned.


input
Resolved data, prior, scheduling, and MCMC settings recorded by the wrapper.



Depending on the implementation, fits can also contain vb, vg, ve, covariance summaries, LD-versus-linkage-equilibrium variance traces, or sampler diagnostics. Use model-specific help for their exact contract.
Compact reporting is preferable to printing complete marker matrices:
data.frame(
  pip_sum = sum(fit$dm[, 1]),
  mean_abs_bm = mean(abs(fit$bm[, 1])),
  mean_vb = mean(fit$vbs[, 1]),
  mean_vg = mean(fit$vgs[, 1]),
  mean_ve = mean(fit$ves[, 1])
)
Useful checks include trace behavior, repeated-chain agreement, sensitivity to priors and scheduling, posterior predictive behavior, top-marker stability, and BED-versus-CSR comparisons where both representations are available. Short workflow chains demonstrate integration; they are not sufficient for final inference. See Workflows and outputs for reporting guidance.

title: Single-Trait Models
text:
Transition to Annotation-Informed Priors
The plain ST-BLR model gives all markers a common active probability () and active-effect variance (v_b). Annotation-informed extensions retain the same regression likelihood and marker-update logic while changing how prior mass or effect scale varies across markers.

Fixed Marker-Specific Priors
stblr_csr_prior_annot() can replace the global values with fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities (_i), variance multipliers, or both:
\[
b_i
\sim
(1-\pi_i)\delta_0
+
\pi_iN(0,v_b\lambda_i).
\]
In the marker update, (_i) replaces the global prior inclusion probability and (v_b_i) replaces the global active-effect variance.


Learned, Group, and Mixture Priors

stblr_csr_learn_annot() learns annotation effects on marker-specific inclusion probabilities and optionally variance multipliers.
stblr_csr_group_annot() gives mutually exclusive marker groups their own inclusion probabilities and variance multipliers.
stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic() uses an SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior, assigning annotation-dependent probabilities to an exact-null component and multiple active variance components.

The SBayesRC-style wrapper is closely aligned with the published SBayesRC prior family but is not an exact reproduction of GCTB SBayesRC as exposed by default. Its default gamma grid and CSR sparse-LD likelihood differ; users can supply the published gamma grid explicitly when that prior grid is desired.
These extensions change the prior architecture, unlike sparse-update scheduling controls. Their definitions, assumptions, diagnostics, and interpretation cautions are developed in Annotation-informed models and Technical annotation priors.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text: This appendix describes how sblr transfers marker annotations into sparse Bayesian linear-regression priors. It develops marker-specific inclusion probabilities and effect-variance scales, explains the fixed, learned, and group-prior CSR wrappers, and records empirical-Bayes constructions from the original annotation-prior draft. The emphasis is on the prior and its implementation contract; the CSR likelihood and sparse-LD representation are covered elsewhere.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Baseline Sparse Prior
For a single trait, the baseline sparse prior introduces a marker inclusion indicator (d_i):
[
\[\begin{aligned}
b_i \mid d_i = 0 &= 0,\\
b_i \mid d_i = 1 &\sim N(0, v_b),\\
\Pr(d_i = 1) &= \pi.
\end{aligned}\]
]
Here (b_i) is the effect of marker (i), (v_b) is the active-marker variance, and () is a global inclusion probability. The posterior inclusion probability (PIP) is
[ (d_i = 1 ), ]
which is summarized by dm when returned by a fitted model.
The annotation-informed models retain this sparse-prior logic but replace one or both global quantities with structured marker-specific quantities:
[ (d_i = 1) = _i, b_i d_i = 1 N(0, v_b w_i), ]
where (w_i > 0) is a marker-specific variance multiplier.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Marker-Specific Prior Construction

Inclusion probabilities
A common annotation construction places annotation effects on the log-odds scale:
[ (_i) = (0) + A_i , ]
where (0) is a baseline inclusion probability and () contains annotation coefficients. Positive values of (A_i_) increase prior inclusion odds; negative values reduce them.
The fixed-prior helper used by the wrappers centers the linear predictor before combining it with the baseline:
[ {i} = A_i- {j=1}^m A_j, _i = ^{-1} {(0)+{i}}. ]
Centering makes the annotation effects primarily redistribute prior inclusion probability across markers rather than changing its genome-wide location. The resulting values are clamped to user-specified lower and upper bounds for numerical and inferential stability.


Effect-variance multipliers
Annotation effects on active-marker variance naturally use a log scale:
[ w_i = A_i_v, w_i = (A_i_v). ]
As with inclusion probabilities, the wrapper centers the linear predictor:
[ _{v i} = A_iv-{j=1}^m A_jv, w_i=({v i}). ]
This construction makes (w_i) a relative multiplier around the global active-marker variance (v_b). Lower and upper bounds prevent extreme annotation combinations from creating nearly degenerate or unreasonably diffuse marker priors.


Consequences for a single-marker update
The marker-specific quantities enter the standard sparse BLR update directly. Let (w_i^{XX}) denote the diagonal marker cross-product and let
[ s_i = r_i + w_i^{XX} b_i ]
be the marker score formed from the current residual state. To avoid confusing the cross-product with the prior multiplier, write (v_{b,i}=v_b w_i). The log Bayes factor for the active versus null component is
[ BF_i = ( ) + {v_e(v_e+w_i^{XX}v_{b,i})}. ]
The conditional inclusion probability is
[ (d_i=1) = . ]
Conditional on inclusion,
[ b_id_i=1, N( , ). ]
Thus, (_i) alters prior odds of inclusion, whereas (w_i) alters the active effect distribution and its shrinkage. These mechanisms should not be interpreted as interchangeable.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Annotation-Level Posterior Summaries
Posterior marker summaries can be aggregated to describe signal associated with an annotation set (S_k={i:A_{ik}}). Useful descriptive summaries include:
[ m_{,k} = _{iS_k}(d_i=1), ]
the expected number of included markers in the set, and the PIP enrichment ratio
[ E_k = {|S_kc|{-1}_{iS_k}(d_i=1)}. ]
For summary-statistics fits, a marker-level contribution estimate may be written
[ c_i = , ]
with an optional PIP-weighted version. An annotation-level genetic-variance summary is then
[ V_{G,k} = _{iS_k} c_i. ]
These set summaries are deliberately descriptive. When annotations overlap, their totals are not additive and the same marker contribution may appear in several sets. summarize_annotation_signal() follows this descriptive set-based approach for known simulation truth and, when a fit is supplied, adds within-set means of dm and absolute bm.
For conditional interpretation with overlapping annotations, one can regress a marker-level posterior response (s_i) on all annotation columns:
[ s_i = + {k=1}^K A{ik}_k+_i. ]
Possible responses include a PIP, squared posterior mean effect, or estimated marker contribution. Such a regression estimates conditional associations among annotations, but it does not establish that an annotation causes the genetic signal.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Empirical-Bayes Prior Construction
An empirical-Bayes workflow estimates annotation signal from one genomic fit and uses it to construct priors for a subsequent fit:
[ {_i,w_i} . ]
This approach separates prior construction from the genomic sampler. It is useful when annotation effects should be estimated with a dedicated model or when fixed marker priors must be inspected before fitting.

Set-based estimates
A smoothed set-level inclusion probability can be estimated from PIPs:
[ _k = , ]
where (a>0) supplies symmetric pseudo-count shrinkage. A rough active-effect variance estimate is
[ v_{b,k} = {(m_{,k},c)}, ]
where (c>0) prevents instability when the expected number of active markers is very small. Both estimates should generally be shrunk toward genome-wide values before they are converted into marker priors.
These formulas are easiest to interpret for disjoint sets. With overlapping annotations, directly assigning each set estimate to its member markers can double-count evidence.


Conditional annotation models
For overlapping annotations, an annotation-level regression or BLR can map marker summaries to annotation coefficients. Candidate marker-level responses from the archived design include:

posterior mean effects, (b_i);
transformed PIPs, such as a bounded ((dm_i));
squared effects or absolute effects; and
marker contribution estimates, (b_i(wy_i-r_i)/n).

The fitted annotation effects can then be transformed through the centered logit and log-scale constructions above. Regularization is essential because annotation columns can be numerous, correlated, imbalanced, or nearly redundant.


Data reuse and cross-fitting
When the same phenotype data are used both to estimate annotation enrichment and to fit the annotation-informed model, the resulting prior is data-dependent. This can improve adaptation but can also exaggerate evidence if uncertainty in the first-stage estimate is ignored.
Useful safeguards include:

shrink annotation coefficients toward zero;
clamp (_i) and (w_i) to defensible ranges;
compare against an unannotated baseline;
split markers into approximately LD-independent folds and construct priors out of fold; and
assess sensitivity to the annotation model and prior bounds.

The current fixed-prior wrapper supports the final marker-prior fitting stage. Cross-fitting and a full empirical-Bayes pipeline remain analysis-level responsibilities rather than a single exported package workflow.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Fixed Marker-Specific Prior Wrapper
stblr_csr_prior_annot() fits a CSR summary-statistics model with fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities and effect-variance multipliers. Users may either supply fixed_pi_marker and fixed_vb_multiplier directly, or supply (A) and fixed annotation coefficients from which the wrapper constructs them.
fit_fixed <- stblr_csr_prior_annot(
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  n = n,
  yy = stats$yy,
  wy = stats$wy,
  ww = stats$ww,
  A = A,
  beta_pi = beta_pi,
  beta_vb = beta_vb
)
The annotation-derived marker priors remain fixed during sampling. Marker effects, inclusion states, residual variance, global variance parameters, and other sampler states may still be updated according to the wrapper’s update flags. Fixed therefore refers to the annotation-to-marker prior mapping, not to the whole fitted model.
This wrapper is appropriate when priors come from external evidence, a separate training analysis, or a deliberately staged empirical-Bayes procedure.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Learned Annotation Effects
stblr_csr_learn_annot() learns annotation coefficients jointly with the marker model. For trait (t), the implemented construction is conceptually
[ (_{it}) = (t) + (A_i{,t}), ]
and
[ v_{b,it} = v_{b,t} {(A_i_{v,t})}. ]
The annotation effects are initialized by eta_pi_init and eta_vb_init, with zero matrices used by default. Gaussian shrinkage scales sigma_eta_pi and sigma_eta_vb regularize the coefficients.
The native sampler uses random-walk Metropolis-Hastings updates at the annot_update_every schedule. The inclusion-coefficient target is informed by the current inclusion states; the variance-coefficient target is informed by the current active effects and inclusion states. Proposal scales are controlled by rw_sd_eta_pi and rw_sd_eta_vb. Marker-level inclusion probabilities and variance multipliers are bounded during construction.
This is a direct learned-prior model rather than a separate two-stage empirical-Bayes fit. The posterior annotation coefficients summarize how the model adapts prior inclusion and active-effect variance, conditional on all other annotations and the sampler specification.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Group Priors
stblr_csr_group_annot() assigns each marker to exactly one group through group_index. Group (g) receives a group-specific inclusion probability and variance multiplier:
[ (d_i=1)={g(i)}, b_id_i=1 N{0,v_b w{g(i)}}. ]
Group inclusion probabilities have beta-prior shape parameters derived from a prior mean and strength. Group variance multipliers may also be updated, depending on updateGroupVb, and can be normalized around a common scale.
The group construction is a simplification of overlapping annotation models: it creates an unambiguous partition and directly pools evidence within groups, but it cannot represent a marker’s simultaneous membership in several functional categories. It is useful when annotations naturally define mutually exclusive strata or when a simpler, more stable model is preferred.
The preparation helper verifies that every marker has one nonmissing group, that requested group names define the ordering, and that every represented group is nonempty. The native interface receives a zero-based group index; users should supply ordinary R group labels and let the wrapper handle that conversion.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Simulation Helpers and Known-Truth Diagnostics
The annotation simulation helpers support controlled checks of whether an annotation-informed model recovers known architecture.
make_overlapping_annotations() creates binary annotation columns using independent membership probabilities. Overlap is allowed, and an option can ensure that every marker belongs to at least one annotation.
make_marker_priors_from_annotations() constructs marker-level inclusion probabilities and variance multipliers from specified enriched annotations. It uses log inclusion-odds and log variance-multiplier effects, optionally centers the linear predictors, and caps the resulting marker priors.
sample_causal_pool_weighted() samples causal markers without replacement, giving markers in selected annotations increased sampling weight.
mtsim_annotation() combines annotation generation, weighted causal-marker sampling, and marker-prior construction with multi-trait phenotype simulation. Its returned truth allows direct comparison of simulated architecture and posterior summaries.
summarize_annotation_signal() reports annotation size, causal-marker counts, and causal rates. If a fit is supplied, it can also report within-annotation mean PIPs and mean absolute posterior marker effects. Because annotation sets may overlap, these summaries should be read one annotation at a time rather than summed across rows.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Overlap, Identifiability, and Double Counting
Overlapping annotations are biologically natural but statistically difficult. If two columns of (A) identify nearly the same markers, their separate coefficients may be weakly identified even when their joint signal is clear. Rare annotations can produce unstable estimates, whereas very broad annotations may largely reproduce the intercept.
Additive constructions on the logit and log scales provide a coherent way to combine overlap:
[ (_i) = (0)+A_i, w_i=A_i_v. ]
However, additive predictors can still create extreme priors when a marker belongs to many enriched sets. Centering, coefficient shrinkage, and explicit bounds are therefore structural safeguards, not merely numerical conveniences.
Interpretation is conditional: an annotation coefficient measures the association remaining after the other included annotations and preprocessing choices are accounted for. Marginal set enrichment and conditional annotation coefficients answer different questions and need not agree.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Research-Stage Multi-Trait Extensions
The archived annotation draft also develops extensions beyond the currently exposed fixed, learned, and group CSR wrappers. They are retained here as design directions rather than claims about the public API.
For multiple traits, marker-specific annotation priors can vary by trait:
[ ({it}) = ({0t})+A_i{,t}, w{it}=A_i_{v,t}. ]
Annotations could also influence cross-trait sharing. For example, a softmax model could assign marker-specific probabilities to patterns such as null, trait-specific, and shared effects. A further extension could let annotation sets influence the covariance of active multi-trait effects. These models require strong regularization because annotation effects, sharing probabilities, and trait covariance can otherwise be difficult to identify.
The draft additionally proposes warm-started regional multi-trait fits: genome-wide annotation summaries construct priors, and selected regions are then fitted with more detailed multi-trait models. Such a workflow may be computationally useful, but prior reuse, region selection, and uncertainty propagation must be handled explicitly.

title: Technical Appendix: Annotation-Informed Priors
text:
Regularization, Bounds, and Uncertainty
Annotation-informed priors add flexibility and therefore add failure modes. The following controls address distinct problems:

Centering separates relative marker enrichment from the genome-wide baseline.
Standardization places quantitative annotations on comparable scales.
Coefficient shrinkage limits overfitting in correlated or high-dimensional annotation matrices.
Probability bounds prevent prior inclusion probabilities from collapsing to zero or one.
Variance-multiplier bounds prevent extreme prior scales.
Cross-fitting or external training reduces optimism from empirical-Bayes data reuse.
Sensitivity analyses reveal dependence on bounds, annotation definitions, LD settings, and prior choices.

Posterior uncertainty conditional on a fixed empirical-Bayes prior does not include uncertainty from estimating that prior. This distinction should be made explicit when reporting results.
