title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
This appendix describes the SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior implemented by stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic(). The core prior family is closely aligned with published SBayesRC: marker effects follow a multi-normal mixture, and marker-specific mixture probabilities are determined by conditional probit stick-breaking regressions on annotations. The exposed sblr model is not an exact reproduction of the published GCTB SBayesRC implementation. Its default gamma grid differs, and it uses a CSR sparse-LD likelihood rather than the GCTB low-rank rotated summary-statistics likelihood.
This note focuses on the annotation-dependent prior and its diagnostics. It does not claim computational equivalence between the two likelihood implementations.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Model Definition
For marker (i), let (z_i {1,,C}) identify one of (C) mixture components. Conditional on (z_i=k), the marker effect is
[ _i z_i=k, v_b, N(0,_k v_b). ]
The vector
[ =(_1,,_C) ]
contains fixed variance multipliers, while (v_b) is the sampled global active-effect variance scale. The implementation requires
[ _1=0, _k>0 k>1. ]
The first component is therefore an exact null component:
[ _i=0 z_i=1. ]
The remaining components represent increasingly diffuse active-effect distributions when their gamma multipliers increase.
For multiple traits supplied to the wrapper, this mixture construction and its annotation coefficients are fitted separately by trait. The formatted fit therefore stores one alpha matrix and one set of marker component summaries per trait.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Gamma Grids
The public sblr default is:
gamma = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
Published SBayesRC uses the five-component grid:
gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
Users can request that published gamma grid explicitly:
fit <- stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic(
  stats = stats,
  ld_prefix = ld_prefix,
  A = A,
  gamma = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
)
Matching the gamma grid aligns this part of the prior specification. It does not make the complete sblr model identical to GCTB SBayesRC because the likelihood, sparse-LD representation, exposed defaults, and implementation details remain distinct.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Annotation-Dependent Component Probabilities
Let (A) be an (m K) marker-by-annotation matrix. For (C) mixture components, let () be a (K (C-1)) coefficient matrix. Column (_j) controls conditional stick-breaking step (j).
For marker (i) and step (j), the linear predictor and conditional continuation probability are
[ {ij}=A_ij, p{ij}=({ij}), ]
where () is the standard normal distribution function. The marker-level component probabilities are
[
\[\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i1} &= 1-p_{i1},\\
\pi_{i2} &= p_{i1}(1-p_{i2}),\\
\pi_{i3} &= p_{i1}p_{i2}(1-p_{i3}),\\
&\ \vdots\\
\pi_{iC} &= \prod_{j=1}^{C-1}p_{ij}.
\end{aligned}\]
]
Equivalently, component (k<C) receives the probability of continuing through all earlier steps and stopping at step (k); the final component receives the probability of continuing through every step.

Why the probabilities sum to one
For a marker with step probabilities (p_1,,p_{C-1}),
[ {k=1}{C}k = (1-p_1) +p_1(1-p_2) ++ ({j=1}{C-2}p_j)(1-p{C-1}) +_{j=1}^{C-1}p_j =1. ]
The expression telescopes: probability either stops at one of the first (C-1) steps or reaches the final component.


Numerical flooring and renormalization
The native sampler computes these probabilities from (A), floors each component probability at pi_floor, and renormalizes each marker row to sum to one. The public default is pi_floor = 1e-12.
Flooring prevents exact numerical zero probabilities when probit predictors are extreme. Because flooring slightly changes the unnormalized stick-breaking probabilities, the subsequent row renormalization is required. This is a numerical-stability adjustment, not a different conceptual link function.
The deterministic R diagnostic helpers apply the mathematical stick-breaking transform without the native sampler’s floor-and-renormalize step. For ordinary finite coefficients, their rows sum to one up to numerical tolerance.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Annotation Matrix and Preprocessing
Rows of (A) must be aligned with the markers in the sufficient statistics, CSR sparse-LD matrix, and posterior outputs. Columns may contain binary or quantitative annotations, and overlap is allowed.
Before fitting, stblr_csr_sbayesrc_generic() calls the shared annotation preparation helper using these controls:

add_intercept = TRUE adds an all-ones first column when one is not already recognized;
standardize_annotations = TRUE centers and scales nonbinary quantitative annotations;
center_binary_annotations = FALSE leaves binary columns unchanged by default;
row names can be used to reorder (A) to known marker names when all names are available.

The preprocessing choices determine the meaning and scale of alpha. Quantitative coefficients are effects per standardized annotation unit under the defaults. An unchanged binary coefficient is a contrast associated with membership in that annotation, conditional on the remaining columns.

Intercept prior
With intercept_flat = TRUE, the first annotation coefficient at every stick-breaking step receives a flat prior in the native alpha update. This assumes the first column is the intercept, which is the arrangement produced when the wrapper adds it. All other annotation coefficients receive the normal prior described below.
If a custom matrix already contains an intercept, place it first when relying on intercept_flat = TRUE. An all-ones column elsewhere in the matrix is not treated as the flat-prior intercept by the native update.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Alpha and SigmaSqAlpha Priors
For non-intercept annotation coefficient (k) at stick-breaking step (j), the implemented prior is
[ {kj}{,j}^2 N(0,_{,j}^2). ]
Each step has its own annotation-effect variance (_{,j}^2), represented by sigmaSqAlpha[j]. Under intercept_flat = TRUE, the first coefficient is excluded from this normal shrinkage prior and from the variance update.
The variance update has scaled-inverse-chi-square or inverse-gamma family form:
[ _{,j}^2 = , ]
where () contains coefficients subject to shrinkage, sigmaSqAlpha_a supplies (a_), and sigmaSqAlpha_b supplies (b_). Both public defaults are 2.
This construction is aligned with the published SBayesRC use of normal annotation-coefficient priors and a scaled-inverse-chi-square-family variance prior. The exact published hyperparameter specification should not be inferred from the sblr defaults. Users should report the values supplied to sigmaSqAlpha_a, sigmaSqAlpha_b, sigmaSqAlpha_init, and intercept_flat.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Gibbs-Style Alpha Updating
When updateAlpha = TRUE, the native sampler updates alpha every alpha_update_every iterations. The public default interval is 10.
The update uses conditional probit data augmentation. At stick-breaking step (j), only markers that reached that step are included. A latent normal variable is sampled for each eligible marker:
[ _{ij}_j N(A_i_j,1), ]
truncated above zero when the marker continues beyond step (j), and truncated at or below zero when it stops at that step.
Conditional on the latent variables and the other coefficients, each annotation coefficient has a normal full conditional. For a non-intercept coefficient, the prior precision (1/_{,j}^2) is added to the data precision. With intercept_flat = TRUE, the first coefficient omits that prior precision. After the coefficients for a step are updated, sigmaSqAlpha[j] is drawn from the scaled-inverse-chi-square-family update.
This is a Gibbs-style conditional update using truncated-normal augmentation and normal draws. It is not a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings alpha update. After an alpha update, the native sampler recomputes all marker-specific prior component probabilities from (A).

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Initialization
make_sbayesrc_alpha_init() creates deterministic initial values for the annotation-dependent mixture architecture.
Given an initial overall active probability pi_init, it distributes active mass across the (C-1) non-null components using normalized active_comp_weights. This produces initial marginal component probabilities
[ ^{(0)} = ( 1-{}, {}w_2, , _{}w_C ). ]
The helper then converts these marginal probabilities to conditional continuation probabilities for the stick-breaking representation. When (A) contains an all-ones column, the first such column receives intercept coefficients
[ _{0j}^{(0)} = {-1}{p_j{(0)}}, ]
and all other coefficients begin at zero. If no all-ones column exists, all default coefficients are zero. Supplied alpha_init and sigmaSqAlpha_init values are accepted after dimension and finite-value validation.
The helper also returns named initial component probabilities, normalized active-component weights, conditional step probabilities, gamma values, and component names. These make initialization auditable without running the sampler.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Marker-Effect and Component Updates
For each marker, the sampler combines the annotation-derived prior component probabilities with the summary-statistics likelihood. The exact null component has (_1=0) and leaves the marker effect at zero. For active component (k), the effect prior variance is
[ v_{b,k}=_k v_b. ]
The sampler forms a component-specific Bayes factor using the current marker score, residual variance, marker diagonal cross-product, and (v_{b,k}). It samples a new component from the resulting posterior component probabilities, then samples the marker effect from its conditional normal distribution when the selected gamma is positive.
The global scale (v_b) may also be updated from currently active marker effects and their selected gamma values when updateB = TRUE. Thus gamma defines relative component scales, while (v_b) supplies the shared sampled scale.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Fit Outputs
The formatted fit exposes the standard marker and variance summaries together with SBayesRC-style architecture summaries.

alpha
fit$alpha is a list with one posterior-mean coefficient matrix per trait. Each matrix has annotations in rows and stick-breaking steps in columns. Because it is a posterior mean, applying a nonlinear probability transform to it gives a plug-in diagnostic, not the posterior mean of that transformed quantity.


sigmaSqAlpha
fit$sigmaSqAlpha is a trait-by-step matrix of posterior mean annotation-effect variance parameters. Large values permit more dispersion among non-intercept annotation coefficients at that stick-breaking step. They should be interpreted together with alpha coefficients, annotation scaling, and chain diagnostics.


comp_prob
fit$comp_prob is a list with one marker-by-component matrix per trait. It contains posterior frequencies of sampled component assignments after burn-in and thinning. It is not the same object as the annotation-derived prior probability matrix computed from (A).


ncomp
fit$ncomp is a trait-by-component matrix containing posterior mean counts of markers assigned to each component. Its row sum should equal the number of markers, subject only to numerical representation.
The usual outputs remain available when returned, including bm, dm, variance traces, covariance summaries, current effects, and residual state. Full marker-scale matrices should be retained for analysis rather than printed in full.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Diagnostic Helpers
Four deterministic exported helpers translate alpha coefficients into compact prior-architecture diagnostics.

Annotation-row diagnostics
sbayesrc_annotation_pi(alpha, gamma) applies the probit stick-breaking transform separately to each row of alpha. It returns an annotation-by-component probability matrix.
sbayesrc_annotation_gamma_mean(alpha, gamma) computes
[ k^{} = {c=1}^{C}_{kc}_c ]
for each alpha row.
These are coefficient-row diagnostics. A binary annotation row, for example, is evaluated as a standalone predictor row. It does not automatically include the fitted intercept or the effects of correlated annotations. It should not be described as the literal component probability for every marker carrying that annotation.


Marker-profile diagnostics
sbayesrc_marker_pi(A, alpha, gamma) first computes (A), then applies the stick-breaking transform. It returns an (m C) marker-level prior component probability matrix.
sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(A, alpha, gamma) computes the plug-in expected gamma for each marker:
[ i^{} = {c=1}^{C}_{ic}_c. ]
These marker-profile helpers include the complete annotation combination in each row of (A). They are generally more directly relevant to the fitted prior architecture than standalone annotation-row summaries.
alpha_t <- fit$alpha[[1]]
prior_pi <- sbayesrc_marker_pi(fit$input$A, alpha_t, fit$input$gamma)
expected_gamma <- sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(
  fit$input$A, alpha_t, fit$input$gamma
)
Because these diagnostics transform posterior mean alpha coefficients, they do not propagate the full posterior uncertainty in alpha. Compact reports can show annotation-row expected gamma, summary(expected_gamma), and the correlation between marker expected gamma and PIP. That correlation describes the fitted prior-posterior relationship; it is not a calibration statistic or causal estimate.

title: Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors
text:
Interpretation of Annotation Effects
An alpha coefficient changes a conditional continuation probability at one stick-breaking step. Its sign cannot be interpreted independently of component ordering:

a positive coefficient increases the probability of continuing past that step;
a negative coefficient increases the probability of stopping at that step;
the consequences for expected gamma depend on all later steps and the gamma grid.

Expected gamma is a useful scalar summary of prior mixture allocation, but it compresses a complete component-probability vector. Two markers can have the same expected gamma while assigning probability to different components. Report component probabilities when those distinctions matter.
Annotation effects and expected-gamma differences are prior-architecture summaries, not proof of biological causality. They can reflect LD, marker density, annotation overlap, quantitative-annotation scaling, model misspecification, and finite-chain behavior. Interpretation should compare annotation-derived prior probabilities with posterior component frequencies and assess sensitivity to preprocessing, gamma grids, sparse-LD settings, and hyperparameters.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
This appendix develops the summary-statistics representation used by sblr from the individual-level linear model. It explains why cross-products are sufficient for BLR-style marker updates, how BED-derived statistics and sparse LD are combined by the CSR samplers, and which assumptions are required for single- and multi-trait analyses.
The central principle is that the Gaussian regression likelihood depends on the observed data through a small set of cross-products. Replacing (X) and (y) with those cross-products can preserve the marker-update algebra, but only when marker order, sample definition, scaling, and LD are compatible.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Individual-Level Model and Cross-Product Sufficiency
For one centered phenotype, consider
[ y=Xb+e, eN(0,v_eI_n), ]
where (X) is an (nm) genotype matrix and (b) is an (m)-vector of marker effects. Conditional on (b) and (v_e), the Gaussian log likelihood is, up to constants,
[ p(yb,v_e) = -(y-Xb)^(y-Xb). ]
Expanding the residual sum of squares gives
[
\[\begin{aligned}
(y-Xb)^\top(y-Xb)
&=
y^\top y
-2b^\top X^\top y
+b^\top X^\top Xb.
\end{aligned}\]
]
Thus, the likelihood does not require repeated access to every individual observation once the following quantities are available:
[ y^y, X^y, X^X, n. ]
The prior can still require additional parameters, but BLR marker likelihood calculations can be expressed through these cross-products. This is the sense in which they are sufficient for the Gaussian regression layer.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Single-Trait Summary-Statistic Notation
For one trait, define
[ wy=X^y, XX=X^X, yy=y^y. ]
The diagonal genotype cross-products are
[ ww_i=XX_{ii}=x_i^x_i. ]
In sblr interfaces:

wy is the marker-phenotype cross-product vector;
ww is the vector containing the diagonal of (XX);
yy is the phenotype sum of squares;
the sparse-LD object represents retained off-diagonal structure; and
(n) is the sample size associated with these quantities.

The dense matrix (XX) can be written as
[ XX=D+O, ]
where (D=(ww)) and (O) contains off-diagonal marker cross-products. The CSR samplers keep (D) explicitly through ww and reconstruct a sparse approximation to (O) from disk-backed LD correlations.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Residual Scores and Marker Updates
Define the marker-scale residual score vector
[ r = X^(y-Xb) = wy-XXb. ]
This is not the individual-level residual vector (y-Xb). It is its projection onto all marker columns.
For marker (i), adding the current marker effect back to its score gives
[ s_i=r_i+ww_i b_i. ]
Because
[ r_i = x_i^y -x_i^x_i b_i -_{ji}x_i^x_jb_j, ]
the quantity (s_i) equals
[ s_i = x_i^y -_{ji}x_i^x_jb_j, ]
which is the marker’s cross-product with the residual excluding its own current effect. BayesC-style inclusion and effect updates depend on (s_i), (ww_i), the residual variance, and prior parameters.
If marker (i)’s effect changes by
[ b_i=b_i{}-b_i{}, ]
then
[ r^{} = r^{}-XX_{i}b_i. ]
The CSR implementation performs the diagonal part directly:
[ r_i^{} = r_i^{}-ww_ib_i, ]
then updates retained LD neighbors using sparse off-diagonal (x_j^x_i) values. This avoids multiplying by a dense (XX) matrix on every marker update.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
The Identity (XXb=wy-r)
Rearranging the residual-score definition gives
[ XXb=wy-r. ]
This identity is useful beyond marker updates. It permits likelihood, genetic-variance, and annotation-contribution calculations from summary statistics and the current marker effects.

Residual sum of squares
Starting from
[ = yy-2bwy+bXXb ]
and substituting (XXb=wy-r) yields
[
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SSE}
&=
yy-2b^\top wy+b^\top(wy-r)\\
&=
yy-b^\top(wy+r).
\end{aligned}\]
]
The single-trait CSR residual-variance update uses this form. It combines yy with the current b, wy, and residual score r without returning to individual-level observations.


Genetic variance
For centered genotypes, the realized genetic value is (g=Xb). Its quadratic form is
[ g^g = b^XXb = b^(wy-r). ]
The corresponding sample-scaled genetic-variance quantity is
[ V_G = b^(wy-r). ]
This is the identity used by the CSR implementation to calculate genetic variance from the current effects and residual scores.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
section: Genotype Scaling, Allele Frequencies, and ww
text:
Genotype Scaling, Allele Frequencies, and ww
Summary statistics and LD are meaningful only relative to the genotype matrix that produced them. Let (g_{ki}{0,1,2}) be the dosage for individual (k) at marker (i), and let (p_i) be the supplied or estimated allele frequency.
With bed_xtx_xty(..., scale = TRUE), the implemented marker coding is
[ x_{ki} = {}. ]
Missing BED genotypes are mapped to zero on this standardized scale, which is mean imputation under the supplied allele frequency. For nondegenerate markers and a compatible sample, the expected marker variance is approximately one, so
[ ww_i=x_i^x_i ]
is often near the number of used individuals. It is not assumed to equal exactly (n): realized allele counts, missingness, external allele frequencies, and sample selection affect it.
With scale = FALSE, the implementation uses raw dosage coding and mean imputes missing values to (2p_i). This path is intentionally uncentered. Consequently, cross-products and regression interpretation differ from the standardized path unless centering is handled elsewhere.
Allele frequencies therefore define more than metadata. They determine the genotype matrix used in wy, ww, and LD. Supplying inconsistent allele frequencies to sufficient-statistic and sparse-LD construction changes the implied (X).

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
section: Dense LD, Correlation LD, and Sparse Cross-Products
text:
Dense LD, Correlation LD, and Sparse Cross-Products
The dense genotype cross-product matrix has entries
[ XX_{ij}=x_i^x_j. ]
Its diagonal is supplied through ww. The disk-backed CSR files produced by the sparse-LD workflow store retained correlations (r_{ij}), not full cross-products. When the CSR sampler reads them, it reconstructs retained off-diagonal cross-products as
[ {ij} = r{ij}. ]
The sampler symmetrizes the retained off-diagonal entries for marker-wise updates. It handles the diagonal separately using ww; diagonal treatment is therefore part of the interface contract and should not be recreated by manually inserting assumed values into the disk files.
With all correlations retained and compatible ww, the reconstruction can represent the corresponding dense (XX). In practice, sparse-LD construction uses thresholds and windows, producing
[ XX. ]
The residual score maintained by the sparse sampler is consequently
[ r = wy-b. ]
Weak or distant omitted LD does not propagate effect changes through this approximate residual score. This approximation is the principal statistical difference between a complete cross-product representation and thresholded CSR LD.
See Technical sparse LD and CSR for storage, thresholding, and disk-contract details.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Computing Statistics With bed_xtx_xty()
bed_xtx_xty() computes sufficient statistics directly from selected markers in one PLINK BED file. A short call is:
stats <- bed_xtx_xty(
  bed_file = Glist$bedfiles[chr],
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = cls,
  af = Glist$af[[chr]][cls],
  y = y,
  rows = NULL,
  scale = TRUE
)
Its principal inputs have the following contracts:

bed_file identifies the PLINK BED file.
n is the number of individuals represented by that BED file.
cls contains positive one-based BED marker indices in the desired model order.
af contains allele frequencies in exactly the cls order. If omitted, the implementation computes frequencies from selected individuals.
y is an (n_{}n_t) phenotype matrix.
rows optionally selects unique one-based BED rows; when supplied, y must contain exactly those selected individuals in that order.
scale selects standardized or raw-dosage marker coding.

For each trait (t), the function returns:
[ wy_t=X^y_t, ww_t=(X^X), yy_t=y_t^y_t. ]
The same ww vector is repeated across traits because the current function uses one selected genotype matrix (X) for all phenotype columns. Additional returned fields include xx, allele frequencies used, row-selection information, sample and marker counts, scaling status, and summaries of marker diagonal cross-products.
The output order is the input cls order. The function does not infer the intended biological marker order from IDs, so that ordering must be established before the call.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Combining bed_xtx_xty() With Sparse LD
The sufficient-statistics and LD branches must describe the same genotype matrix:
same BED marker selection and order
+ same selected individuals
+ same allele frequencies and scaling
    -> compatible wy, ww, yy, and sparse LD
sparseLD_stream_CSR() constructs retained marker correlations from BED data and writes them under ld_prefix. It must receive the same marker ordering, sample rows, allele frequencies, and scaling convention used to create the sufficient statistics.
The central workflow handoff is:
BED + phenotype
  -> bed_xtx_xty()        -> wy, ww, yy, n
  -> sparseLD_stream_CSR() -> ld_prefix
  -> stblr_csr()
The complete operational sequence is documented in Sparse-LD and BED workflows.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Multi-Trait Summary-Statistic Notation
For (n_t) traits, collect phenotypes in
[ Y=
\[\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 & \cdots & y_{n_t}
\end{bmatrix}\]
]
and marker effects in an (mn_t) matrix
[ B=
\[\begin{bmatrix}
b_1 & \cdots & b_{n_t}
\end{bmatrix}\]
. ]
The individual-level model is
[ Y=XB+E_Y, ]
where the rows of (E_Y) may have residual covariance matrix (_e). The central multi-trait cross-products are
[ WY=X^Y ]
and
[ SSY=Y^Y. ]
Column (t) of (WY) is (wy_t=X^y_t). Entry (SSY_{ts}=y_t^y_s) is the observed cross-trait phenotype product among individuals shared by traits (t) and (s).
For a common (X), define the marker-score matrix
[ R=X^(Y-XB)=WY-XXB. ]
Trait by trait,
[ XXb_t=wy_t-r_t. ]
This permits a symmetric genetic covariance estimate:
[ G_{ts} = . ]
When (t=s), this reduces to the single-trait genetic-variance expression. When all traits use the same (n), the denominator becomes (n).

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
section: Cross-Trait Phenotype Products and Sample Overlap
text:
Cross-Trait Phenotype Products and Sample Overlap
The diagonal of SSY contains the single-trait values:
[ SSY_{tt}=yy_t. ]
The off-diagonals contain information not recoverable from separate yy values:
[ SSY_{ts} = {iI{ts}}y_{it}y_{is}, ]
where (I_{ts}) is the set of individuals observed for both traits. These terms are required for a full residual covariance update because
[ (Y-XB)^(Y-XB) = SSY -Y^XB -BXY +B^XXB. ]
With individual-level data, SSY and overlap counts are directly observable. With summary statistics, they must be supplied or reconstructed. If (N_{ts}=|I_{ts}|) and the cross-trait phenotype covariance is (_{ts}), then under random missingness and covariance homogeneity,
[ E(SSY_{ts})=N_{ts}_{ts}. ]
Given phenotype correlations (R_y) and approximate trait variances
[ (y_t) , ]
one can form
[ {ts} = R{y,ts} ]
and reconstruct
[ = N(Y), ]
forcing the diagonal to the observed yy values.
Full-overlap and fractional-overlap assumptions define different (N) matrices and therefore different reconstructed likelihood information. Missing or incorrect cross-trait information limits residual covariance inference even when every trait has valid marginal summary statistics. The complete derivation and sensitivity considerations belong in Technical multi-trait sample overlap.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
section: Residual and Genetic Covariance From Summary Scores
text:
Residual and Genetic Covariance From Summary Scores
For a joint multi-trait model, the residual cross-product matrix can be constructed from SSY, (WY), current effects, and residual scores. One orientation is
[ S_e = SSY -B^WY -WY^B +B^XXB. ]
Using (XXB=WY-R),
[ S_e = SSY -B^WY -WY^B +B^(WY-R). ]
Finite precision, asymmetric inputs, or trait-specific constructions can make cross-trait expressions differ slightly by orientation. The native multi-trait CSR implementation symmetrizes off-diagonal residual and genetic covariance quantities before covariance updates.
These calculations require a compatible definition of (X), trait sample sizes, and cross-trait phenotype products. A vector of per-trait yy values supports separate trait-wise residual variance updates; it does not by itself identify a full residual covariance matrix.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Set-Specific and Weighted Genetic Contributions
The identity (XXb_t=wy_t-r_t) also supports marker-set summaries. For a marker set (S_k), define
[ V_{G,k,t} = {iS_k} b{it}(wy_{it}-r_{it}). ]
The corresponding marker-level contribution is
[ c_{it} = . ]
An optional posterior-inclusion-weighted version is
[ c^{}_{it} = . ]
These are useful descriptive summaries for annotations or genomic regions. For disjoint sets, their sums can approximate a partition of the fitted genetic-variance expression. For overlapping sets, a marker contributes to every set containing it, so set totals are attributions rather than an additive partition.
The formulas also mix posterior summaries nonlinearly when posterior mean bm, PIP dm, and a returned residual score are combined. They should not be confused with exact posterior expectations unless calculated draw by draw.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Validation and Diagnostics
Before fitting a summary-statistics model, check:

Every trait’s wy vector has length (m).
Every trait’s ww vector has length (m), contains finite positive values, and is compatible with the LD scaling.
yy has one value per trait for parallel single-trait fitting, or SSY is a valid (n_tn_t) matrix for a full joint multi-trait likelihood.
The supplied (n) is the sample size used to calculate the corresponding statistics; trait-specific (n_t) values and overlap assumptions are recorded where relevant.
Sparse-LD dimensions equal (mm), and its marker order matches wy and ww.
cls, allele frequencies, rows, and scale choices match between bed_xtx_xty() and sparse-LD construction.
Marker names, annotation rows, and posterior output rows use the same order.
Phenotypes are centered or the intercept/centering convention is otherwise explicit.
ww magnitude is plausible for the coding and sample size.
LD thresholds, windows, precision, and reference-sample provenance are recorded.

Useful diagnostics include inspecting stats$n, stats$m, stats$scale, stats$min_xx, stats$mean_xx, and stats$max_xx; reading CSR metadata with sparseLD_read_CSR(); and comparing BED-direct and CSR fits when the same individual-level data are available.

title: Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics
text:
Limitations
Summary-statistics inference cannot recover information that was not retained or supplied.

LD compatibility: wy and ww from one sample or scaling convention combined with LD from another imply an approximate and potentially biased likelihood.
LD-reference mismatch: ancestry, allele frequencies, imputation quality, marker filtering, and sample selection can make reference LD differ from study LD.
Sparsification: thresholding and windowing deliberately remove off-diagonal information.
Phenotype preprocessing: unrecorded centering, scaling, covariate adjustment, or residualization changes the meaning of wy and yy.
Multi-trait information: marginal trait statistics do not identify cross-trait phenotype products or sample overlap.
Overlap assumptions: incorrect (N) or phenotype covariance assumptions can distort full residual covariance inference.
Posterior summaries: set contributions calculated from posterior means do not automatically propagate full posterior uncertainty.

These limitations should be treated as model-input assumptions, not merely implementation details.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
In sparse Bayesian regression models fitted to genome-wide summary statistics, single-trait Bayesian linear regression (STBLR) can be used as a stable first-stage model. The resulting posterior marker summaries, especially posterior mean marker effects and posterior inclusion probabilities, can then be used to inform a second-stage multi-trait Bayesian linear regression (MTBLR) model.
The main idea is to use first-stage posterior summaries together with marker annotations or marker sets to construct annotation-informed prior parameters. These parameters can then be used in later STBLR or MTBLR analyses.
Typical first-stage outputs are:
\[
\hat b_{it} = E(b_{it} \mid \text{data}),
\]
and
\[
\widehat{dm}_{it} = P(d_{it}=1 \mid \text{data}),
\]
where marker \(i = 1, \ldots, m\) and trait \(t = 1, \ldots, T\).
Let \(A\) denote an annotation matrix:
\[
A_{ik} =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if marker } i \text{ belongs to annotation } k, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The annotation columns may overlap. For example, a marker may be coding, close to a gene, and located inside a QTL region at the same time.
The goal is to derive annotation-specific or marker-specific prior parameters such as:
\[
\pi_{k,t}, \qquad \sigma^2_{b,k,t}, \qquad B_k, \qquad \pi_{k,m},
\]
where \(k\) indexes an annotation class or marker set, \(t\) indexes a trait, and \(m\) indexes a multi-trait sharing model.

annotation_lm_vg <- function(fit, annot, trait, n) {
  b <- fit$bm[, trait]
  q <- fit$wy[, trait] - fit$r[, trait]

  y <- b * q / n
  X <- as.data.frame(annot)

  lm(y ~ ., data = X)
}

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
9.1 R implementation
estimate_annotation_vb <- function(fit, sets, n, min_eff = 1, shrink = 0.5) {
  b  <- fit$bm
  dm <- fit$dm
  q  <- fit$wy - fit$r

  nt <- ncol(b)
  K <- length(sets)

  vb_ann <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)
  vg_ann <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)
  meff   <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)

  rownames(vb_ann) <- rownames(vg_ann) <- rownames(meff) <- names(sets)
  colnames(vb_ann) <- colnames(vg_ann) <- colnames(meff) <- colnames(b)

  for (k in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[k]]

    for (t in seq_len(nt)) {
      vg <- sum(b[idx, t] * q[idx, t]) / n
      neff <- sum(dm[idx, t])

      vg_ann[k, t] <- max(vg, 0)
      meff[k, t] <- neff
      vb_ann[k, t] <- max(vg_ann[k, t] / max(neff, min_eff), 1e-12)
    }
  }

  # Shrink annotation-specific scales toward a global scale.
  vb_global <- colMeans(vb_ann, na.rm = TRUE)

  for (t in seq_len(nt)) {
    vb_ann[, t] <- shrink * vb_ann[, t] + (1 - shrink) * vb_global[t]
  }

  list(vb = vb_ann, vg = vg_ann, meff = meff)
}

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
10.1 R implementation
derive_marker_vb_from_annotation_model <- function(global_vb, annot, gamma,
                                                   cap = c(0.25, 4)) {
  # annot: m x K annotation matrix
  # gamma: K x nt annotation coefficients on log scale
  # global_vb: length nt

  eta <- annot %*% gamma
  vb_marker <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(annot), ncol(gamma))

  for (t in seq_len(ncol(gamma))) {
    mult <- exp(eta[, t])
    mult <- pmin(pmax(mult, cap[1]), cap[2])
    vb_marker[, t] <- global_vb[t] * mult
  }

  colnames(vb_marker) <- colnames(gamma)
  vb_marker
}

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
12.1 R implementation
estimate_annotation_B <- function(bm, dm, sets, ridge = 1e-8, shrink = 0.5) {
  nt <- ncol(bm)
  K <- length(sets)

  B_list <- vector("list", K)
  names(B_list) <- names(sets)

  # Global covariance from posterior mean effects.
  w_global <- pmax(apply(dm, 1, max), 1e-6)
  B_global <- crossprod(bm * sqrt(w_global)) / sum(w_global)
  B_global <- B_global + diag(ridge, nt)

  for (k in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[k]]
    w <- pmax(apply(dm[idx, , drop = FALSE], 1, max), 1e-6)

    Bk <- crossprod(bm[idx, , drop = FALSE] * sqrt(w)) / sum(w)
    Bk <- shrink * Bk + (1 - shrink) * B_global
    Bk <- 0.5 * (Bk + t(Bk))
    diag(Bk) <- pmax(diag(Bk), ridge)

    B_list[[k]] <- Bk
  }

  B_list
}

Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
15.1 Stage 1: STBLR genome-wide screening
Run STBLR for each trait to obtain:
\[
\hat b_{it}, \qquad \widehat{dm}_{it}, \qquad r_{it}.
\]
These are used to estimate annotation effects, variance contributions, and sharing patterns.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
15.2 Stage 2: Annotation summary and decomposition
Compute:
\[
\widehat V_{G,k,t},
\]
PIP enrichment,
\[
\text{enrichment}_{k,t},
\]
and, if desired, fit annotation-level STBLR or MTBLR models.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
15.3 Stage 3: Derive prior parameters
Estimate:
\[
\pi_{k,t},
\]
\[
\sigma^2_{b,k,t},
\]
\[
B_k,
\]
and
\[
\pi_{k,m}.
\]
For overlapping annotations, derive marker-specific priors using log-linear or logistic annotation models.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
15.4 Stage 4: Annotation-informed STBLR or MTBLR
Use the derived priors in a second-stage model:
\[
b_{it} \sim (1-\pi_{it})\delta_0 + \pi_{it}N(0, v_{b,it})
\]
for STBLR, or
\[
\mathbf b_i \sim \sum_m \pi_{i,m} N_m(0, B_i)
\]
for MTBLR.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.1 First-stage genomic fit
The first-stage genomic model is fitted using the ordinary summary-statistic inputs:
\[
wy, \quad ww, \quad yy, \quad LD.
\]
It produces marker-level posterior summaries:
\[
\hat b_{it}, \qquad dm_{it}, \qquad r_{it}, \qquad q_{it}=wy_{it}-r_{it}.
\]
Here \(\hat b_{it}\) is the posterior mean marker effect, \(dm_{it}\) is the posterior inclusion probability, and \(q_{it}\) is the fitted marker score implied by the current posterior mean effects.
Useful marker-level response matrices include:
\[
S^{(b)}_{it} = \hat b_{it},
\]
\[
S^{(pip)}_{it} = \operatorname{logit}(dm_{it}),
\]
and
\[
S^{(vg)}_{it}
=
\frac{\hat b_{it}(wy_{it}-r_{it})}{n}.
\]
The third response is LD-aware and directly related to the marker-level contribution to genomic variance.
In R:
S_b <- fit0$bm
S_pip <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(fit0$dm, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6))
S_vg <- fit0$bm * (fit0$wy - fit0$r) / n

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.2 Annotation-level STBLR
Let \(A\) be the marker-by-annotation matrix. A single-trait annotation model is:
\[
S_t = A\gamma_t + e_t,
\]
where \(S_t\) is one column of a marker-level response matrix, and \(\gamma_t\) is a vector of annotation effects for trait \(t\).
Using a BayesC-like prior,
\[
\gamma_{kt} = \delta_{kt}\alpha_{kt},
\]
\[
\delta_{kt} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{\gamma,t}),
\]
and
\[
\alpha_{kt} \mid \delta_{kt}=1
\sim
N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma,t}).
\]
The annotation-level STBLR posterior gives:
\[
E(\gamma_{kt} \mid S),
\]
and
\[
P(\delta_{kt}=1 \mid S).
\]
These quantities measure whether annotation \(k\) explains marker-level evidence for trait \(t\), conditional on other overlapping annotations.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.3 Annotation-level MTBLR
For multiple traits, use:
\[
S = A\Gamma + E,
\]
where \(S\) is an \(m \times T\) marker-level response matrix and \(\Gamma\) is a \(K \times T\) matrix of annotation effects.
For annotation \(k\):
\[
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k
=
(\gamma_{k1},\ldots,\gamma_{kT})^\top.
\]
An MTBLR prior can be used to infer annotation sharing patterns:
\[
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k
\sim
\sum_m \pi_{\gamma,m} N_m(0, B_\gamma),
\]
where \(m\) indexes trait-sharing models such as:
000, 100, 010, 001, 110, 101, 011, 111
for three traits. The posterior model probabilities indicate whether an annotation contributes to one trait, several traits, or all traits.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.4 Deriving marker-specific inclusion priors
From an annotation model fitted to \(S^{(pip)}\), construct a marker-specific annotation score:
\[
\eta_{it}
=
\eta_{0t} + \sum_k A_{ik}\hat\gamma_{kt}.
\]
Then transform it to a marker-specific prior inclusion probability:
\[
\pi_{it}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta_{it}).
\]
The annotation contribution should usually be centered so the genome-wide mean prior inclusion probability remains close to the original base rate.
derive_pi_marker <- function(A, gamma, base_pi, cap = c(1e-8, 0.05)) {
  A <- as.matrix(A)
  gamma <- as.matrix(gamma)

  eta <- A %*% gamma

  # Center annotation contribution so the genome-wide mean stays near base_pi.
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, colMeans(eta, na.rm = TRUE), "-")
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, qlogis(base_pi), "+")

  pi_marker <- plogis(eta)
  pmin(pmax(pi_marker, cap[1]), cap[2])
}
A reasonable base rate is:
base_pi <- colMeans(fit0$dm)
Then:
pi_marker <- derive_pi_marker(
  A = annot,
  gamma = fitAnn_pip$bm,
  base_pi = base_pi,
  cap = c(1e-8, 0.05)
)
In the next genomic STBLR, marker \(i\) and trait \(t\) use \(\pi_{it}\) instead of a global \(\pi_t\).

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.5 Deriving marker-specific prior effect variances
From an annotation model fitted to \(S^{(vg)}\) or \(S^{(b^2)}\), construct marker-specific prior effect variances:
\[
\log v_{b,it}
=
\log v_{b,t}^{global}
+
\sum_k A_{ik}\hat\theta_{kt}.
\]
Thus:
\[
v_{b,it}
=
v_{b,t}^{global}
\exp\left(\sum_k A_{ik}\hat\theta_{kt}\right).
\]
Again, the annotation contribution should be centered and capped.
derive_vb_marker <- function(A, theta, global_vb, cap = c(0.25, 4)) {
  A <- as.matrix(A)
  theta <- as.matrix(theta)

  eta <- A %*% theta
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, colMeans(eta, na.rm = TRUE), "-")

  mult <- exp(eta)
  mult <- pmin(pmax(mult, cap[1]), cap[2])

  vb_marker <- sweep(mult, 2, global_vb, "*")
  pmax(vb_marker, 1e-12)
}
For example:
global_vb <- colMeans(fit0$vbs)

vb_marker <- derive_vb_marker(
  A = annot,
  theta = fitAnn_vg$bm,
  global_vb = global_vb,
  cap = c(0.25, 4)
)
These marker-specific prior variances can be used in the next genomic STBLR by replacing the global \(v_b\) with \(v_{b,it}\).

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.6 Deriving MTBLR marker-specific sharing-model priors
For MTBLR, annotation-level MTBLR can be used to derive marker-specific priors over sharing models.
Let \(\eta_{km}\) be the annotation-level effect of annotation \(k\) on sharing model \(m\). Then for marker \(i\):
\[
\log \pi_{im}
=
\log \pi_m^{global}
+
\sum_k A_{ik}\eta_{km}.
\]
Normalize across models:
\[
\pi_{im}
=
\frac{\exp(\log \pi_{im})}
{\sum_l \exp(\log \pi_{il})}.
\]
derive_model_pi_marker <- function(A, eta_model, base_pi, eps = 1e-12) {
  A <- as.matrix(A)
  eta_model <- as.matrix(eta_model)

  log_pi <- A %*% eta_model
  log_pi <- sweep(log_pi, 2, colMeans(log_pi, na.rm = TRUE), "-")
  log_pi <- sweep(log_pi, 2, log(pmax(base_pi, eps)), "+")

  log_pi <- sweep(log_pi, 1, apply(log_pi, 1, max), "-")
  pi_marker <- exp(log_pi)
  pi_marker <- sweep(pi_marker, 1, rowSums(pi_marker), "/")

  pmax(pi_marker, eps)
}
In the genomic MTBLR C++ marker sampler, this changes the model prior term from:
loglik[k] = std::log(pi[k]) - 0.5 * logdet + 0.5 * quad;
to:
loglik[k] = std::log(pi_marker(i, k)) - 0.5 * logdet + 0.5 * quad;
This allows annotations to influence whether a marker is more likely to be trait-specific or pleiotropic.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
section: 20.7 Deriving a global MTBLR prior covariance matrix from annotations
text:
20.7 Deriving a global MTBLR prior covariance matrix from annotations
An annotation-level MTBLR also gives annotation effect estimates across traits. These can be used to estimate a global prior covariance matrix for the next genomic MTBLR run.
Let \(\hat\Gamma\) be the matrix of annotation posterior mean effects. A weighted covariance estimate is:
\[
B_{ann}
=
\frac{\sum_k w_k \hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_k^\top}
{\sum_k w_k},
\]
where \(w_k\) can be an annotation-level posterior inclusion weight, for example:
\[
w_k = \max_t dm^{ann}_{kt}.
\]
estimate_B_from_annotation_model <- function(gamma, dm, ridge = 1e-8) {
  gamma <- as.matrix(gamma)
  w <- pmax(apply(dm, 1, max), 1e-6)

  B <- crossprod(gamma * sqrt(w)) / sum(w)
  B <- 0.5 * (B + t(B))
  diag(B) <- pmax(diag(B), ridge)

  B
}
This matrix can be used as the initial global \(B\) matrix in the next MTBLR run.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.8 Recommended empirical-Bayes workflow
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Round 1: genomic STBLR or MTBLR
# ------------------------------------------------------------
fit0 <- stblr_cpg_omp_csr(...)
# or:
# fit0 <- mtblr_cpg_omp_csr(...)

# Marker-level responses
S_b   <- fit0$bm
S_pip <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(fit0$dm, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6))
S_vg  <- fit0$bm * (fit0$wy - fit0$r) / n

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Round 2: annotation-level STBLR or MTBLR
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Here annot is the marker-by-annotation design matrix.
fitAnn_pip <- stblr_annotation(
  y = S_pip,
  X = annot
)

fitAnn_vg <- stblr_annotation(
  y = S_vg,
  X = annot
)

# Optional multi-trait annotation model.
fitAnn_mt <- mtblr_annotation(
  Y = S_vg,
  X = annot,
  models = models
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Derive annotation-informed genomic priors
# ------------------------------------------------------------
pi_marker <- derive_pi_marker(
  A = annot,
  gamma = fitAnn_pip$bm,
  base_pi = colMeans(fit0$dm),
  cap = c(1e-8, 0.05)
)

vb_marker <- derive_vb_marker(
  A = annot,
  theta = fitAnn_vg$bm,
  global_vb = colMeans(fit0$vbs),
  cap = c(0.25, 4)
)

B_init <- estimate_B_from_annotation_model(
  gamma = fitAnn_mt$bm,
  dm = fitAnn_mt$dm
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Round 3: genomic STBLR or MTBLR with annotation-informed priors
# ------------------------------------------------------------
fit1 <- stblr_cpg_omp_csr(
  ...,
  pi_marker = pi_marker,
  vb_marker = vb_marker
)

fit1_mt <- mtblr_cpg_omp_csr(
  ...,
  B = B_init,
  pi_marker_model = pi_marker_model,
  adjE = 0.9
)

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.9 Interpretation
The annotation-level BLR or MTBLR does not estimate marker effects directly. It estimates how annotations explain marker-level evidence from the first genomic model. The resulting priors are therefore empirical-Bayes priors. They are useful for stabilizing later genomic analyses, improving initialization, guiding sharing-model probabilities, and incorporating biological information.
The most useful derived quantities are:
\[
\pi_{it},
\]
marker-specific inclusion probabilities,
\[
v_{b,it},
\]
marker-specific prior effect variances,
\[
\pi_{im},
\]
marker-specific MTBLR sharing-model probabilities, and
\[
B_{ann},
\]
an annotation-informed global MTBLR prior covariance matrix.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
20.10 Cross-fitting and overfitting
Because the same data may be used to estimate marker summaries and then to construct priors, the procedure is empirical Bayes and can be optimistic if used for formal inference. A more conservative strategy is chromosome-wise cross-fitting:
for (chr in chromosomes) {
  # 1. Fit or summarize annotation model using all chromosomes except chr.
  # 2. Derive priors for markers on chr.
  # 3. Refit genomic STBLR or MTBLR on chr using those priors.
}
This avoids using the same markers both to estimate their annotation-informed priors and to evaluate their posterior evidence.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.1 Direct annotation-informed STBLR
In a single-trait BayesC-style STBLR model, marker effects can be written as:
\[
b_{it} = d_{it}\alpha_{it},
\]
where
\[
d_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{it}),
\]
and
\[
\alpha_{it} \mid d_{it}=1 \sim N(0, v_{b,it}).
\]
The annotation matrix can be used to model the prior inclusion probability as:
\[
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{it}) = \mu_{\pi,t} + A_i \eta_{\pi,t},
\]
where \(\eta_{\pi,t}\) is a vector of annotation effects on inclusion probability for trait \(t\).
Similarly, the marker-specific prior effect variance can be modelled as:
\[
\log(v_{b,it}) = \mu_{v,t} + A_i \eta_{v,t}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
v_{b,it} = \exp(\mu_{v,t} + A_i\eta_{v,t}).
\]
This gives an annotation-aware STBLR model:
\[
b_{it} \sim (1-\pi_{it})\delta_0 + \pi_{it}N(0,v_{b,it}).
\]
This is a direct extension of the usual global-prior STBLR model, where all markers share the same \(\pi_t\) and \(v_{b,t}\).

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.2 Modified STBLR marker update
For marker \(i\), define the partial residual score:
\[
s_{it} = r_{it} + w_{it}b_{it},
\]
where \(w_{it}=x_i^\top x_i\) for trait \(t\).
With marker-specific prior variance \(v_{b,it}\) and residual variance \(v_{e,t}\), the Bayes factor for inclusion becomes:
\[
\log BF_{it}
=
\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{v_{e,t}}{v_{e,t}+w_{it}v_{b,it}}\right)
+
\frac{1}{2}\frac{s_{it}^2v_{b,it}}{v_{e,t}(v_{e,t}+w_{it}v_{b,it})}.
\]
The posterior inclusion probability is:
\[
P(d_{it}=1 \mid -)
=
\frac{\pi_{it}BF_{it}}{(1-\pi_{it})+\pi_{it}BF_{it}}.
\]
Conditional on inclusion, the posterior draw is:
\[
b_{it} \mid d_{it}=1,- \sim N(m_{it}, s^2_{it}),
\]
where
\[
m_{it} = \frac{s_{it}}{w_{it}+v_{e,t}/v_{b,it}},
\]
and
\[
s^2_{it} = \frac{v_{e,t}}{w_{it}+v_{e,t}/v_{b,it}}.
\]
Thus, the only change in the existing STBLR sampler is to replace the global \(\pi_t\) and \(v_{b,t}\) by marker-specific values \(\pi_{it}\) and \(v_{b,it}\).
A corresponding C++ change is conceptually:
const double pi1 = pi_marker(i);
const double pi0 = 1.0 - pi1;
const double vbi = vb_marker(i);

const double denom = ve + wi * vbi;

const double logBF =
  0.5 * std::log(ve / denom) +
  0.5 * score * score * vbi / (ve * denom);

const double lhs = wi + ve / vbi;
const double mean = score / lhs;
const double sd = std::sqrt(ve / lhs);
For multiple traits running in parallel STBLR, \(\pi_{it}\) and \(v_{b,it}\) can be stored as marker-by-trait matrices:
const double pi1 = pi_marker(i, t);
const double vbi = vb_marker(i, t);

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
section: 21.3 Estimating annotation effects inside the sampler
text:
21.3 Estimating annotation effects inside the sampler
There are two main ways to handle the annotation coefficients \(\eta_{\pi,t}\) and \(\eta_{v,t}\).

21.3.1 Fixed annotation effects
The simplest approach is to estimate \(\eta_{\pi,t}\) and \(\eta_{v,t}\) before the genomic sampler, for example from a previous STBLR/MTBLR annotation analysis, and then treat them as fixed during the next genomic run.
This gives a stable empirical-Bayes model:
\[
\widehat\eta_{\pi,t}, \widehat\eta_{v,t}
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\pi_{it}, v_{b,it}
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\text{annotation-informed genomic STBLR}.
\]
This is the easiest and safest implementation.


21.3.2 Updating annotation effects during sampling
A more ambitious approach is to update the annotation effects inside the sampler. For example, one could place priors on annotation effects:
\[
\eta_{\pi,kt} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\eta_\pi,t}),
\]
and
\[
\eta_{v,kt} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\eta_v,t}).
\]
The sampler would then alternate between:

marker-effect updates using current \(\pi_{it}\) and \(v_{b,it}\),
annotation-effect updates using current marker inclusion states \(d_{it}\) and marker effects \(b_{it}\),
variance component updates.

For inclusion probabilities, the annotation update can be viewed as a Bayesian logistic regression:
\[
d_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{it}),
\]
with
\[
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{it}) = \mu_{\pi,t} + A_i\eta_{\pi,t}.
\]
For effect variances, active marker effects can inform a log-variance regression:
\[
\log(b_{it}^2 + \epsilon) \approx \mu_{v,t} + A_i\eta_{v,t} + e_{it},
\]
using only markers with \(d_{it}=1\), or using weights based on posterior inclusion probabilities.
This fully Bayesian version is more elegant, but also more complicated and more prone to mixing issues. For implementation, it is usually better to start with fixed annotation-derived priors.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.4 Direct annotation-informed MTBLR
In MTBLR, each marker has a vector of trait effects:
\[
\mathbf b_i = (b_{i1},\ldots,b_{iT})^\top.
\]
The usual MTBLR model uses a set of sharing models \(M_m\). For example, with three traits the model space may be:
\[
000, 100, 010, 001, 110, 101, 011, 111.
\]
A direct annotation-aware MTBLR model lets the annotation profile \(A_i\) determine the prior probability of each sharing model:
\[
P(M_i=m \mid A_i) = \pi_{im}.
\]
A convenient parameterization is a multinomial-logit model:
\[
\log \pi_{im} = c_m + A_i\eta_m - C_i,
\]
where \(C_i\) is the normalizing constant:
\[
C_i = \log\left(\sum_l \exp(c_l + A_i\eta_l)\right).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\pi_{im}
=
\frac{\exp(c_m + A_i\eta_m)}
{\sum_l \exp(c_l + A_i\eta_l)}.
\]
The annotation matrix can therefore make coding markers more likely to follow a shared model, promoter markers more likely to be trait-specific, or QTL markers more likely to have non-null effects across several traits.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
section: 21.5 MTBLR model prior in the marker update
text:
21.5 MTBLR model prior in the marker update
In the MTBLR marker sampler, the model posterior weight for marker \(i\) and model \(m\) typically has the form:
\[
\log w_{im}
=
\log \pi_m + \log L_{im},
\]
where \(\log L_{im}\) is the marginal likelihood contribution under sharing model \(m\).
With annotation-informed marker-specific model priors, this becomes:
\[
\log w_{im}
=
\log \pi_{im} + \log L_{im}.
\]
Thus, the existing sampler only needs to replace the global model prior \(\pi_m\) with marker-specific priors \(\pi_{im}\).
In C++ this corresponds to replacing:
loglik[k] = std::log(pi[k]) - 0.5 * logdet + 0.5 * quad;
with:
loglik[k] = std::log(pi_marker_model(i, k)) - 0.5 * logdet + 0.5 * quad;
This is likely the most useful direct annotation extension for MTBLR, because it lets annotations guide the sharing model while still allowing the multivariate likelihood to override the prior when the data are strong.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.6 Annotation-informed MTBLR effect covariance
Annotations can also affect the prior covariance matrix of marker effects. A global MTBLR model may use:
\[
\mathbf b_i \mid M_i=m \sim N_m(0,B),
\]
where \(N_m(0,B)\) denotes a multivariate normal distribution restricted to the active traits in model \(m\).
An annotation-aware version can use marker-specific or annotation-specific covariance matrices:
\[
\mathbf b_i \mid M_i=m,A_i \sim N_m(0,B_i).
\]
A log-linear construction for trait-specific prior variances is:
\[
\log B_{i,tt} = \mu_{B,t} + A_i\eta_{B,t}.
\]
For cross-trait covariances, one can either use a global correlation matrix \(R\) and annotation-specific standard deviations:
\[
B_i = D_i R D_i,
\]
where
\[
D_i = \mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{B_{i,11}},\ldots,\sqrt{B_{i,TT}}),
\]
or use annotation-specific full covariance matrices \(B_k\).
The first approach is more stable:
\[
B_i = D_i R D_i.
\]
It lets annotations change the amount of prior variance per trait while preserving a globally estimated cross-trait correlation structure.
The second approach is more flexible:
\[
B_i = \sum_k w_{ik}B_k,
\]
where \(w_{ik}\) are normalized annotation weights for marker \(i\). However, this can be unstable if annotations are sparse or highly overlapping.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
section: 21.7 Direct annotation-aware STBLR and MTBLR as hierarchical models
text:
21.7 Direct annotation-aware STBLR and MTBLR as hierarchical models
The direct annotation model can be summarized as a hierarchical prior.
For STBLR:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{it}) &= \mu_{\pi,t} + A_i\eta_{\pi,t}, \\
\log(v_{b,it}) &= \mu_{v,t} + A_i\eta_{v,t}, \\
d_{it} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{it}), \\
b_{it} \mid d_{it}=1 &\sim N(0,v_{b,it}), \\
b_{it} \mid d_{it}=0 &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
For MTBLR:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{im}
&=
\frac{\exp(c_m + A_i\eta_m)}
{\sum_l \exp(c_l + A_i\eta_l)}, \\
M_i &\sim \mathrm{Categorical}(\pi_{i1},\ldots,\pi_{iM}), \\
\mathbf b_i \mid M_i=m,A_i &\sim N_m(0,B_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
These formulations are direct annotation-informed genomic models rather than post hoc annotation analyses.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.8 Practical implementation strategy
A good implementation path is incremental.

21.8.1 Step 1: Fixed marker-specific priors
First, compute \(\pi_{it}\), \(v_{b,it}\), and \(\pi_{im}\) outside the sampler, then pass them as inputs:
fit <- stblr_cpg_omp_csr(
  ...,
  pi_marker = pi_marker,
  vb_marker = vb_marker
)

fit_mt <- mtblr_cpg_omp_csr(
  ...,
  pi_marker_model = pi_marker_model
)
This only requires small changes to the marker-update functions.


21.8.2 Step 2: Annotation matrix as input, fixed annotation coefficients
Instead of passing full marker-specific prior matrices, pass the annotation matrix and annotation coefficients:
fit <- stblr_cpg_omp_csr(
  ...,
  annot = A,
  eta_pi = eta_pi,
  eta_vb = eta_vb
)
Then compute marker-specific priors inside C++:
\[
\pi_{it} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\mu_{\pi,t}+A_i\eta_{\pi,t}),
\]
and
\[
v_{b,it} = \exp(\mu_{v,t}+A_i\eta_{v,t}).
\]
This saves memory if \(m\) is large and the annotation matrix is sparse.


21.8.3 Step 3: Update annotation coefficients
Finally, update \(\eta_{\pi,t}\), \(\eta_{v,t}\), or \(\eta_m\) inside the sampler. This creates a fully hierarchical annotation-informed BLR/MTBLR model, but requires additional MCMC steps, careful priors, and good diagnostics.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.10 Centering, shrinkage, and caps
Direct annotation priors can be powerful but need regularization. The annotation contribution should usually be centered so that it redistributes prior mass rather than changing the total prior sparsity too aggressively.
For inclusion probabilities:
\[
\eta_{it}^{centered}
=
A_i\eta_{\pi,t}
-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m A_j\eta_{\pi,t}.
\]
Then:
\[
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{it})
=
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_t^{global})+
\eta_{it}^{centered}.
\]
For prior variances:
\[
\log(v_{b,it})
=
\log(v_{b,t}^{global})+
\xi_{it}^{centered},
\]
where
\[
\xi_{it}^{centered}
=
A_i\eta_{v,t}
-
\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m A_j\eta_{v,t}.
\] The resulting multipliers should be capped:
\[
\frac{v_{b,it}}{v_{b,t}^{global}} \in [c_{min},c_{max}],
\]
for example:
\[
[c_{min},c_{max}] = [0.25,4].
\]
Similarly, marker-specific inclusion probabilities should be bounded:
\[
\pi_{it} \in [\epsilon, \pi_{max}],
\]
for example:
\[
\epsilon = 10^{-8}, \qquad \pi_{max}=0.05.
\]
These constraints prevent a highly enriched annotation from overwhelming the likelihood or causing too many markers to enter the model.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.11 Recommended first direct model
The most practical first direct annotation model is:
\[
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{it}) = \mathrm{logit}(\pi_t^{global}) + A_i\eta_{\pi,t}^{centered},
\]
with a global \(v_{b,t}\) unchanged.
For MTBLR, the most practical first model is:
\[
\log \pi_{im} = \log \pi_m^{global} + A_i\eta_m^{centered} - C_i.
\]
These two extensions are simple, interpretable, and likely to be stable. Marker-specific prior variances \(v_{b,it}\) and marker-specific covariance matrices \(B_i\) are useful next steps, but they should be introduced with shrinkage and caps.

title: Annotation-Informed Prior Scales for STBLR and MTBLR
text:
21.12 Causal interpretation and causal-hypothesis generation
The annotation-informed STBLR/MTBLR framework can provide evidence for genetic sharing, annotation enrichment, and plausible biological mechanisms, but it does not by itself identify causal relationships in the intervention sense. The model can estimate posterior quantities such as
\[
P(d_{it}=1 \mid \text{data}),
\]
where \(d_{it}\) indicates that marker \(i\) is active for trait \(t\), and in the multivariate case
\[
P(M_i=m \mid A_i, \text{data}),
\]
where \(M_i\) is a trait-sharing model and \(A_i\) denotes the annotation profile of marker \(i\). These are statements about which genetic effects and annotation patterns best explain the observed summary statistics. They are not, by themselves, causal effects such as
\[
\text{annotation} \rightarrow \text{trait},
\]
or
\[
\text{trait 1} \rightarrow \text{trait 2}.
\]
A careful interpretation is that the model identifies annotations, regions, and marker-sharing configurations that are enriched for genetic signal. For example, if annotation \(A\) has high posterior support for shared effects on traits \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), then the model supports the statement
\[
A \text{ is enriched for shared genetic effects on } t_1 \text{ and } t_2.
\]
This is a genetic-architecture statement, not a direct causal claim. It can, however, motivate causal hypotheses about biological mechanisms.

21.12.1 Genetic sharing versus causal direction
MTBLR can help distinguish different forms of genetic sharing. For example, a marker may support a sharing model such as
\[
M_i = 110,
\]
which indicates an effect on traits 1 and 2 but not trait 3. If this sharing pattern is enriched in annotation \(A\), then
\[
P(M_i=110 \mid A_i, \text{data})
\]
may be larger than the genome-wide background probability. This suggests that annotation \(A\) may tag a biological mechanism relevant to both traits.
However, this does not determine whether the relationship is
\[
G \rightarrow t_1 \rightarrow t_2,
\]
or
\[
G \rightarrow t_2 \rightarrow t_1,
\]
or horizontal pleiotropy,
\[
G \rightarrow t_1
\quad \text{and} \quad
G \rightarrow t_2,
\]
through separate biological pathways. Additional information is required to infer directionality.


21.12.2 What can be inferred directly
The framework can directly support posterior statements such as:
\[
P(\text{marker } i \text{ is active for trait } t \mid \text{data}),
\]
\[
P(\text{marker } i \text{ has a shared effect across traits} \mid \text{data}),
\]
\[
P(\text{annotation } k \text{ is enriched for effects} \mid \text{data}),
\]
and
\[
P(M_i=m \mid A_i, \text{data}).
\]
These quantities can be used to prioritize markers, regions, annotations, and biological pathways for downstream causal analyses. They should be interpreted as posterior evidence for association and sharing, not as proof of causation.


21.12.3 Connection to colocalization
A natural downstream analysis is colocalization. Suppose a genomic region shows a strong MTBLR sharing signal between a molecular trait \(x\) and a complex trait \(y\). If fine-mapping and colocalization support the same causal variant for both traits, then this strengthens the hypothesis
\[
G \rightarrow x \rightarrow y.
\]
In this setting, annotation-aware MTBLR can be used as a prioritization step. It can identify regions and annotations where shared effects are likely, and colocalization can then test whether the same underlying variant is responsible for the molecular and complex-trait associations.


21.12.4 Connection to Mendelian randomization
Mendelian randomization can be used to test directional hypotheses such as
\[
x \rightarrow y,
\]
using genetic variants as instruments. The validity of this interpretation depends on instrumental-variable assumptions. In particular, the genetic instruments should be associated with the exposure, should not be associated with confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship, and should affect the outcome only through the exposure.
Annotation-aware MTBLR can help select or classify candidate instruments. For example, variants that appear trait-specific for exposure \(x\) may be more useful as instruments than variants with strong evidence of broad horizontal pleiotropy. Conversely, markers assigned to shared-effect models may indicate biological pleiotropy and should be handled carefully in causal analyses.


21.12.5 Annotation-specific causal hypotheses
The most useful causal-hypothesis output from the framework may be annotation-specific sharing probabilities. For example, for annotation \(k\), one can estimate
\[
P(M=110 \mid A_k=1, \text{data}),
\]
or compare it to the background probability
\[
P(M=110 \mid \text{data}).
\]
If
\[
P(M=110 \mid A_k=1, \text{data})
>
P(M=110 \mid \text{data}),
\]
then annotation \(k\) is enriched for variants with shared effects on traits 1 and 2. This can motivate a biological hypothesis that the functional class represented by annotation \(k\) is involved in a mechanism linking the two traits.
Similarly, if annotation \(k\) is enriched for trait-specific models, such as
\[
M=100,
\]
then the annotation may be more relevant to a trait-specific pathway than to a shared pathway.


21.12.6 Practical causal workflow
A practical workflow is:

Fit STBLR or MTBLR using GWAS summary statistics and sparse LD.
Estimate marker-level posterior summaries such as \(bm\), \(dm\), and sharing-model probabilities.
Use annotation-aware STBLR/MTBLR to identify annotations enriched for trait-specific or shared genetic effects.
Use the enriched annotations and regions to define candidate mechanisms.
Perform regional fine-mapping to construct credible sets.
Test colocalization with molecular QTL data, such as expression, methylation, protein, metabolite, or microbiome QTL.
Use Mendelian randomization, mediation analysis, perturbation data, or experimental validation to test directional causal hypotheses.

Thus, the annotation-informed STBLR/MTBLR framework is best viewed as a mechanism-discovery and hypothesis-prioritization layer. It can point to annotations and regions that are likely to be biologically relevant, but causal interpretation requires additional assumptions or external evidence.
A suitable manuscript statement is:

The annotation-informed STBLR/MTBLR framework identifies annotations and genomic regions enriched for trait-specific or shared genetic effects. These results can prioritize plausible causal mechanisms and candidate mediators. However, causal interpretation requires additional assumptions or complementary analyses, such as fine-mapping, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, mediation analysis, perturbation experiments, or external functional validation.
